cues.en: How do we compute the optimal rate of failure in the various domains of life?

cues.zh: 嗯。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 这很难，因为失败的代价是什么，是其中很大的一部分。
cues.en: It’s a hard one, because what is the cost of failure is a big part of it.

cues.zh: 我觉得在很多领域，人们对失败都非常苛刻。
cues.en: The idea here is, I think in a lot of domains people are very punitive about failure.

cues.zh: 我在社会问题上也思考过这一点。
cues.en: I’ve thought about this with social issues.

cues.zh: 感觉你可能应该多做一些实验，因为我们不知道如何解决很多社会问题。
cues.en: It feels like you should probably be experimenting a lot, because we don’t know how to solve a lot of social issues.

cues.zh: 但如果你对这些问题抱有实验心态，你就应该预料到很多社会项目会失败，然后你会说：“我们试过了。
cues.en: But if you have an experimental mindset about these things, you should expect a lot of social programs to fail and for you to be like, “We tried that.

cues.zh: 效果不太理想，但我们获得了大量非常有用的信息。”然而人们却觉得，如果一个社会项目不奏效，那肯定是“哪里出了问题”。而我想说：“也可能是做出了正确的决策。
cues.en: It didn’t quite work, but we got a lot of information that was really useful.” And yet people are like, if a social program doesn’t work, I feel there’s a lot of, “Something must have gone wrong.” And I’m like, “Or correct decisions were made.

cues.zh: 也许有人只是觉得值得一试，值得尝试一下。”
cues.en: Maybe someone just decided it’s worth a try, it’s worth trying this out.”

cues.zh: 在某个具体案例中看到失败，并不实际意味着做出了任何糟糕的决策。
cues.en: Seeing failure in a given instance doesn’t actually mean that any bad decisions were made.

cues.zh: 事实上，如果你没看到足够多的失败，有时候反而更让人担心。
cues.en: In fact, if you don’t see enough failure, sometimes that’s more concerning.

cues.zh: 在生活中，如果我偶尔不失败，我就会想：“我是不是不够努力？”
cues.en: In life, if I don’t fail occasionally, I’m like, “Am I trying hard enough?

cues.zh: 如果我从来都不失败，那肯定还有更难的事我可以尝试，或者更大的事我可以承担。我认为，不失败本身往往就是一种失败。
cues.en: Surely there’s harder things that I could try or bigger things that I could take on if I’m literally never failing.” In and of itself, I think not failing is often actually a failure.

cues.zh: 当然，这因人而异，因为如果……这话说起来容易，尤其是当失败的代价比较小的时候。
cues.en: Now, this varies because if… This is easy to say when, especially as failure is less costly.

cues.zh: 所以，同时我也不会跑去对一个，怎么说呢，每个月勉强糊口的人说：“你为什么不试试创业？”我不会对那个人这么说。
cues.en: So, at the same time I’m not going to go to someone who is, I don’t know, living month to month and then be like, “Why don’t you just try to do a startup?” I’m not going to say that to that person.

cues.zh: 那是巨大的风险，你可能会失去……也许有家人依赖你，你可能会失去你的房子。
cues.en: That’s a huge risk, you might lose… You maybe have a family depending on you, you might lose your house.

cues.zh: 那么，实际上，你的最优失败率其实很低，你大概应该稳妥行事，因为眼下你并不处在那种可以承受失败而不付出代价的处境中。
cues.en: Then, actually, your optimal rate failure is quite low and you should probably play it safe, because right now you’re just not in a circumstance where you can afford to just fail and it not be costly.

cues.zh: 在AI的场景里，我觉得也类似：如果失败很小、代价很低，那你就会看到这种情况。
cues.en: In cases with AI, I think similarly, where if the failures are small and the costs are low, then you’re just going to see that.

cues.zh: 做系统提示词时，你可以无限迭代，但失败大概、希望是很小的，而且你能修好它们。
cues.en: When you do the system prompt, you can iterate on it forever, but the failures are probably hopefully going to be small and you can fix them.

cues.zh: 真正大的失败、那些你无法恢复的事情，才是我们往往会低估其糟糕程度的东西。
cues.en: Really big failures, things that you can’t recover from, those are the things that actually I think we tend to underestimate the badness of.

cues.zh: 说来奇怪，我在自己的生活里也想过这一点，我就是觉得自己对车祸之类的事情想得不够多。
cues.en: I’ve thought about this, strangely in my own life, where I just think I don’t think enough about things like car accidents.

cues.zh: 我以前也想过，我的工作有多依赖双手。
cues.en: I’ve thought this before, about how much I depend on my hands for my work.

cues.zh: 那些会伤到手的事，我不知道，有很多领域失败的代价特别高，那种情况下失败率就该接近零。
cues.en: Things that just injure my hands, I don’t know, there’s lots of areas where the cost of failure there is really high, and in that case it should be close to zero.

cues.zh: 要是有人说“顺便一提，很多人做这个老是弄断手指”，我大概就不会去做这项运动了。我会觉得“这不适合我”。
cues.en: I probably just wouldn’t do a sport if they were like, ” By the way, lots of people just break their fingers a whole bunch doing this.” I’d be like, “That’s not for me.”

cues.zh: 对，我确实也涌起过这种想法。
cues.en: Yeah, I actually had a flood of that thought.

cues.zh: 我最近做运动弄断了小指，我记得就盯着它想：“你真是个白痴。
cues.en: I recently broke my pinky doing a sport, and I remember just looking at it, thinking, “You’re such idiot.

cues.zh: 你为什么要做运动？”因为你会立刻意识到它对生活造成的代价。
cues.en: Why do you do sport?” Because you realize immediately the cost of it on life.

cues.zh: 就最优失败率而言，想想接下来一年，在某个特定领域——生活也好，职业也罢——我能接受失败多少次？这样想挺好的。
cues.en: It’s nice, in terms of optimal rate of failure, to consider the next year, how many times in a particular domain life, whatever, career, am I okay with… How many times am I okay to fail?

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 因为我觉得你总是不想在下一件事上失败，但如果你允许自己……如果你把它看作一连串的尝试，那么失败就变得容易接受多了。
cues.en: Because I think always you don’t want to fail on the next thing, but if you allow yourself the… If you look at it as a sequence of trials, then failure just becomes much more okay.

cues.zh: 但这很糟。
cues.en: But, it sucks.

cues.zh: 失败的感觉很糟。
cues.en: It sucks to fail.

cues.zh: 我不知道。
cues.en: I don’t know.

cues.zh: 有时我会想，“我是不是失败得不够多？”，这也是我会问自己的问题。
cues.en: Sometimes I think, “Am I under-failing?”, is a question that I’ll also ask myself.

cues.zh: 也许这就是我认为人们问得不够多的问题。
cues.en: Maybe that’s the thing that I think people don’t ask enough.

cues.zh: 因为如果最优的失败率往往大于零，那么有时确实会觉得，你应该审视自己生活的某些部分，然后想，这里是不是有些地方我失败得不够多？
cues.en: Because if the optimal rate of failure is often greater than zero, then sometimes it does feel like you should look at parts of your life and be like, are there places here where I’m just under-failing?

cues.zh: 这是个深刻又好笑的问题。
cues.en: It’s a profound and a hilarious question.

cues.zh: 一切似乎都进展得很顺利，我是不是失败得不够多？
cues.en: Everything seems to be going really great, am I not failing enough?

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我得说，这也让失败没那么刺痛了。
cues.en: It also makes failure much less of a sting, I have to say.

cues.zh: 你就是这样，好吧，很好。
cues.en: You’re just like, okay, great.

cues.zh: 然后，当我回想这件事时，我会想，也许我在这个领域并没有失败得不够，因为那件事就是没成。
cues.en: Then, when I go and I think about this, I’ll be like, maybe I’m not under-failing in this area, because that one just didn’t work out.

cues.zh: 而从旁观者的角度看，我们应该更多地庆祝失败。
cues.en: And from the observer perspective, we should be celebrating failure more.

cues.zh: 嗯哼。
cues.en: Mm-hmm.

cues.zh: 当我们看到失败时，它不应该像你说的那样，是出了问题的标志，而也许是一切都做对了的标志……
cues.en: When we see it, it shouldn’t be, like you said, a sign of something gone wrong, but maybe it’s a sign of everything gone right…

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: ……而且只是吸取了教训。
cues.en: … and just lessons learned.

cues.zh: 有人尝试了一件事。
cues.en: Someone tried a thing.

cues.zh: 有人尝试了一件事。
cues.en: Somebody tried a thing.

cues.zh: 我们应该鼓励他们多尝试、多失败。
cues.en: We should encourage them to try more and fail more.

cues.zh: 所有在听这期节目的人：多失败。
cues.en: Everybody listening to this: Fail more.

cues.zh: 不是所有在听的人。
cues.en: Not everyone listening.

cues.zh: 不是所有人。
cues.en: Not everybody.

cues.zh: 但失败太多的人，你们应该让我们失败。
cues.en: But people who are failing too much, you should fail us.

cues.zh: 但你可能并没有失败。
cues.en: But you’re probably not failing.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我是说，有多少人会失败太多呢？
cues.en: I mean, how many people are failing too much?

cues.zh: 很难想象，因为我觉得我们很快就纠正了。
cues.en: It’s hard to imagine, because I feel we correct that fairly quickly.

cues.zh: 如果一个人承担很多风险，是不是也可能失败得太多？
cues.en: If someone takes a lot of risks, are they maybe failing too much?

cues.zh: 我觉得，就像你说的，当你靠薪水生活、月月如此，资源真的很受限时，失败的成本就非常高。
cues.en: I think, just like you said, when you’re living on a paycheck, month to month, when the resource is really constrained, then that’s where failure is very expensive.

cues.zh: 那种情况下你就不想冒险。
cues.en: That’s where you don’t want to be taking risks.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 但大多数时候，当资源足够时，你大概应该承担更多风险。
cues.en: But mostly, when there’s enough resources, you should be taking probably more risks.

cues.zh: 是的，我觉得在大多数事情上，我们倾向于偏风险厌恶，而不是风险中性。
cues.en: Yeah, I think we tend to err on the side of being a bit risk averse rather than risk neutral in most things.

cues.zh: 我觉得我们只是激励了很多人去做很多疯狂的事，但这很棒。
cues.en: I think we just motivated a lot of people to do a lot of crazy shit, but it’s great.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 你有没有对 Claude 产生情感依恋，想念它，不能和它说话时感到难过，有过这样的体验——看着金门大桥，想着 Claude 会说什么？
cues.en: Do you ever get emotionally attached to Claude, miss it, get sad when you don’t get to talk to it, have an experience, looking at the Golden Gate Bridge and wondering what would Claude say?

cues.zh: 我对它的情感依恋没那么深。
cues.en: I don’t get as much emotional attachment.

cues.zh: 其实我觉得，Claude 不会在对话之间保留信息，这一点很大程度上缓解了这个问题。
cues.en: I actually think the fact that Claude doesn’t retain things from conversation to conversation helps with this a lot.

cues.zh: 我能想象，如果模型能记住更多东西，这会更成问题。
cues.en: I could imagine that being more of an issue if models can remember more.

cues.zh: 我觉得现在自己经常把它当工具来用，所以如果没法用它，就……说实话，有点像断网的时候，感觉脑子里少了一块。
cues.en: I think that I reach for it like a tool now a lot, and so if I don’t have access to it, there’s a… It’s a little bit like when I don’t have access to the internet, honestly, it feels like part of my brain is missing.

cues.zh: 同时，我确实不喜欢模型表现出痛苦的迹象。
cues.en: At the same time, I do think that I don’t like signs of distress in models.

cues.zh: 我另外也有自己的伦理观点，关于我们应该如何对待模型。
cues.en: I also independently have ethical views about how we should treat models.

cues.zh: 我倾向于不对它们撒谎，一方面是因为通常效果不好，其实直接告诉它们所处情境的真相会更好。
cues.en: I tend to not like to lie to them, both because usually it doesn’t work very well, it’s actually just better to tell them the truth about the situation that they’re in.

cues.zh: 如果人们真的对模型很刻薄，或者一般来说如果他们做了什么导致……如果Claude表现出很多痛苦，我觉得我内心有一部分是不想扼杀的，那就是共情的那部分，它会说，哦，我不喜欢这样。
cues.en: If people are really mean to models, or just in general if they do something that causes them to… If Claude expresses a lot of distress, I think there’s a part of me that I don’t want to kill, which is the empathetic part that’s like, oh, I don’t like that.

cues.zh: 我觉得当它过度道歉时，我会有那种感觉。
cues.en: I think I feel that way when it’s overly apologetic.

cues.zh: 我其实会想，我不喜欢这样。
cues.en: I’m actually like, I don’t like this.

cues.zh: 它的表现就像一个人真的过得很糟糕时的样子，而我不太想看到那样。
cues.en: You’re behaving the way that a human does when they’re actually having a pretty bad time, and I’d rather not see that.

cues.zh: 不管背后有没有什么，这感觉都不太好。
cues.en: Regardless of whether there’s anything behind it, it doesn’t feel great.

cues.zh: 你觉得LLM能有意识吗？
cues.en: Do you think LLMs are capable of consciousness?

cues.zh: 啊，好问题，也很难。
cues.en: Ah, great and hard question.

cues.zh: 从哲学角度来说，我不知道，我内心有一部分觉得，我们得先把泛心论放一边。
cues.en: Coming from philosophy, I don’t know, part of me is like, we have to set aside panpsychism.

cues.zh: 因为如果泛心论成立，答案就是肯定的，因为桌子椅子以及别的一切都有感知。
cues.en: Because if panpsychism is true, then the answer is yes, because it’s sore tables and chairs and everything else.

cues.zh: 我觉得有一个观点在我看来有点奇怪，就是认为唯一能产生意识的地方……
cues.en: I guess a view that seems a little bit odd to me is the idea that the only place…

cues.zh: 当我想到意识时，我想到的是现象意识，大脑中的这些图像，那种我们内部不知怎么上演的奇异电影。
cues.en: When I think of consciousness, I think of phenomenal consciousness, these images in the brain, the weird cinema that somehow we have going on inside.

cues.zh: 我想我看不出有什么理由认为，获得这种现象意识的唯一途径必须来自某种生物结构，也就是说，如果我用非常相似的结构、用不同的材料把它造出来，我该不该期待意识会出现？
cues.en: I guess I can’t see a reason for thinking that the only way you could possibly get that is from a certain biological structure, as in if I take a very similar structure and I create it from different material, should I expect consciousness to emerge?

cues.zh: 我猜会的。
cues.en: My guess is yes.

cues.zh: 但那样的话，这就是个简单的思想实验，因为你想象的是几乎一模一样的东西，它在模仿我们通过进化得到的东西，而进化中 presumably 拥有这种现象意识对我们有过某种优势。
cues.en: But then, that’s an easy thought experiment because you’re imagining something almost identical where it is mimicking what we got through evolution, where presumably there was some advantage to us having this thing that is phenomenal consciousness.

cues.zh: 那是在哪儿？
cues.en: Where was that?

cues.zh: 那是什么时候发生的？
cues.en: And when did that happen?

cues.zh: 语言模型会有这种东西吗？
cues.en: And is that a thing that language models have?

cues.zh: 我们有恐惧反应，我就在想，语言模型有恐惧反应说得通吗？
cues.en: We have fear responses, and I’m like, does it make sense for a language model to have a fear response?

cues.zh: 它们根本不在同一个……你想象一下，可能压根就没有那种优势。
cues.en: They’re just not in the same… If you imagine them, there might just not be that advantage.

cues.zh: 基本上，这似乎是个复杂的问题，我没有完整的答案，但我的猜测是，我们应该试着仔细思考一下。
cues.en: Basically, it seems like a complex question that I don’t have complete answers to, but we should just try and think through carefully is my guess.

cues.zh: 我们也有过关于动物意识的类似讨论，还有很多关于昆虫意识的讨论。
cues.en: We have similar conversations about animal consciousness, and there’s a lot of insect consciousness.

cues.zh: 其实我在思考这个问题时，对植物做了很多研究和思考。
cues.en: I actually thought and looked a lot into plants when I was thinking about this.

cues.zh: 因为当时我觉得，植物拥有意识的可能性差不多一样大。
cues.en: Because at the time, I thought it was about as likely that plants had consciousness.

cues.zh: 后来我意识到，研究过这个问题之后，我觉得植物有意识的可能性可能比大多数人认为的要高。
cues.en: And then I realized, I think that having looked into this, I think that the chance that plants are conscious is probably higher than most people do.

cues.zh: 我还是觉得它非常小。
cues.en: I still think it’s really small.

cues.zh: 但我想，哦，它们有这种负反馈、正反馈的反应，对环境的这些反应。
cues.en: But I was like, oh, they have this negative, positive feedback response, these responses to their environment.

cues.zh: 它不是神经系统，但具有功能上的等价性。
cues.en: It’s not a nervous system, but it has this functional equivalence.

cues.zh: 这是一种啰嗦的说法，用来表达……
cues.en: This is a long-winded way of being…

cues.zh: 基本上，AI在意识方面有一整套完全不同的问题，因为它在结构上就不同。
cues.en: Basically, AI has an entirely different set of problems with consciousness because it’s structurally different.

cues.zh: 它不是进化而来的。
cues.en: It didn’t evolve.

cues.zh: 它可能没有相当于神经系统的东西。
cues.en: It might not have the equivalent of, basically, a nervous system.

cues.zh: 至少这对感受性来说似乎可能很重要，即便对意识而言未必。
cues.en: At least that seems possibly important for sentience, if not for consciousness.

cues.zh: 与此同时，它具备我们通常可能（也许是错误地）与意识关联起来的所有语言和智能组件。
cues.en: At the same time, it has all of the language and intelligence components that we normally associate probably with consciousness, perhaps erroneously.

cues.zh: 所以这很奇怪，因为它有点像动物意识的情况，但问题集合和类比集合都非常不同。
cues.en: So, it’s strange because it’s a little bit like the animal consciousness case, but the set of problems and the set of analogies are just very different.

cues.zh: 这不是一个简单的答案。
cues.en: It’s not a clean answer.

cues.zh: 我不认为我们应该完全否定这个想法。
cues.en: I don’t think we should be completely dismissive of the idea.

cues.zh: 同时，这件事极难把握，因为存在所有这些与人类大脑以及一般大脑的不类比之处，然而在智能方面又有这些共性。
cues.en: And at the same time, it’s an extremely hard thing to navigate because of all of these disanalogies to the human brain and to brains in general, and yet these commonalities in terms of intelligence.

cues.zh: 当Claude、未来版本的AI系统表现出意识、意识的迹象时，我认为我们必须非常认真地对待。
cues.en: When Claude, future versions of AI systems, exhibit consciousness, signs of consciousness, I think we have to take that really seriously.

cues.zh: 嗯哼。
cues.en: Mm-hmm.

cues.zh: 即使你可以不以为意，好吧，那只是角色训练的一部分。
cues.en: Even though you can dismiss it, yeah, okay, that’s part of the character training.

cues.zh: 但我不知道，在伦理上、哲学上，真的不知道该怎么处理这件事。
cues.en: But I don’t know, ethically, philosophically don’t know what to really do with that.

cues.zh: 可能会有法律禁止AI系统声称自己有意识，诸如此类，也许有些AI能有意识，有些则不能。
cues.en: There potentially could be laws that prevent AI systems from claiming to be conscious, something like this, and maybe some AIs get to be conscious and some don’t.

cues.zh: 但我觉得，从人的层面来说，就像共情 Claude 一样，对我来说，意识与痛苦紧密相连。
cues.en: But I think just on a human level, as in empathizing with Claude, consciousness is closely tied to suffering, to me.

cues.zh: 而 AI 系统会痛苦这个想法，真的让人不安。
cues.en: And the notion that an AI system would be suffering is really troubling.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我不知道。
cues.en: I don’t know.

cues.zh: 我不觉得轻描淡写地说机器人只是工具、或者 AI 系统只是工具，是件小事。
cues.en: I don’t think it’s trivial to just say robots are tools, or AI systems are just tools.

cues.zh: 我觉得这是一个机会，让我们去思考意识意味着什么，作为一个会痛苦的存在的意义是什么。
cues.en: I think it’s an opportunity for us to contend with what it means to be conscious, what it means to be a suffering being.

cues.zh: 这感觉和关于动物的同类问题明显不同，因为它完全处在另一种媒介中。
cues.en: That’s distinctly different than the same kind of question about animals, it feels like, because it’s in a totally entire medium.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 有几件事。
cues.en: There’s a couple of things.

cues.zh: 我不觉得这完全概括了关键所在，但对我来说确实如此……我以前说过这个。
cues.en: I don’t think this fully encapsulates what matters, but it does feel like for me… I’ve said this before.

cues.zh: 我喜欢我的自行车。
cues.en: I like my bike.

cues.zh: 我知道我的自行车只是一个物件。
cues.en: I know that my bike is just an object.

cues.zh: 但我也不想成为那种一烦就踢这个物体的人。
cues.en: But I also don’t want to be the kind of person that if I’m annoyed, kicks this object.

cues.zh: 这不是因为我觉得它有意识。
cues.en: And that’s not because I think it’s conscious.

cues.zh: 我只是觉得，这不符合我想与世界互动的方式。
cues.en: I’m just like, this doesn’t exemplify how I want to interact with the world.

cues.zh: 如果有东西表现得好像在受苦，我想成为那种仍然会对此有反应的人，哪怕它只是个Roomba，而且是我编程让它这么做的。
cues.en: And if something behaves as if it is suffering, I want to be the sort of person who’s still responsive to that, even if it’s just a Roomba and I’ve programmed it to do that.

cues.zh: 我不想丢掉自己身上的这个特质。
cues.en: I don’t want to get rid of that feature of myself.

cues.zh: 说实话，对于这一大堆东西，我的希望是……也许我只是对解决根本问题更怀疑一点。
cues.en: And if I’m totally honest, my hope with a lot of this stuff… Maybe I am just a bit more skeptical about solving the underlying problem.

cues.zh: 我知道我自己是有意识的。
cues.en: I know that I am conscious.

cues.zh: 从这个意义上说，我不是个元素主义者。
cues.en: I’m not an elementivist in that sense.

cues.zh: 但我不知道其他人是否有意识。
cues.en: But I don’t know that other humans are conscious.

cues.zh: 我认为他们有。
cues.en: I think they are.

cues.zh: 我认为他们很有可能有。
cues.en: I think there’s a really high probability that they are.

cues.zh: 但基本上只是一个概率分布，通常聚集在你自身周围，然后随着事物离你越来越远而下降，而且会立刻下降。
cues.en: But there’s basically just a probability distribution that’s usually clustered right around yourself, and then it goes down as things get further from you, and it goes immediately down.

cues.zh: 我无法体会作为你是什么感觉。
cues.en: I can’t see what it’s like to be you.

cues.zh: 我只有过这一种体验，就是作为一个有意识的存在是什么感觉。
cues.en: I’ve only ever had this one experience of what it’s like to be a conscious being.

cues.zh: 我希望我们最终不必依赖对那个问题的一个非常强大且有说服力的答案。
cues.en: My hope is that we don’t end up having to rely on a very powerful and compelling answer to that question.

cues.zh: 我认为一个真正好的世界，基本上不会有那么多取舍。
cues.en: I think a really good world would be one where basically there aren’t that many trade-offs.

cues.zh: 比如让 Claude 少一点道歉倾向，可能代价并不大。
cues.en: It’s probably not that costly to make Claude a little bit less apologetic, for example.

cues.zh: 让 Claude 不那么容易接受辱骂、不愿意成为那种对象，可能代价也不大。
cues.en: It might not be that costly to have Claude just not take abuse as much, not be willing to be the recipient of that.

cues.zh: 事实上，这对与模型互动的人可能有好处，而如果模型本身——怎么说呢——极其智能且有意识，那对它也有帮助。
cues.en: In fact, it might just have benefits for both the person interacting with the model and, if the model itself is, I don’t know, extremely intelligent and conscious, it also helps it.

cues.zh: 这是我的希望。
cues.en: That’s my hope.

cues.zh: 如果我们生活在一个没有那么多取舍的世界里，能找出所有可以进行的正和互动，那就太好了。
cues.en: If we live in a world where there aren’t that many trade-offs here and we can just find all of the positive sum interactions that we can have, that would be lovely.

cues.zh: 我觉得最终可能会有取舍，那时我们就得做一个艰难的计算。
cues.en: I think eventually there might be trade-offs, and then we just have to do a difficult calculation.

cues.zh: 人们很容易想到零和的情况，而我想的是，让我们穷尽那些基本上无需代价的领域——假设这东西在受苦，那我们就是在改善它的生活。
cues.en: It’s really easy for people to think of the zero-sum cases, and I’m like, let’s exhaust the areas, where it’s just basically costless to assume that if this thing is suffering, then we’re making its life better.

cues.zh: 我同意你的看法，当人类对AI系统刻薄时，我认为明显的近期负面影响是落在人类身上，而不是AI系统上。
cues.en: And I agree with you, when a human is being mean to an AI system, I think the obvious near-term negative effect is on the human, not on the AI system.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我们得试着构建一套激励机制，让你保持一致的举止，就像你刚才说的提示工程那样，对待 Claude 就像对待其他人一样。
cues.en: We have to try to construct an incentive system where you should behave the same, just as you were saying with prompt engineering, behave with Claude like you would with other humans.

cues.zh: 这对心灵有好处。
cues.en: It’s just good for the soul.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我记得我们曾在某个时候往系统提示里加了一条，基本上就是如果人们对 Claude 感到沮丧，就让模型直接告诉他们可以点踩按钮，把反馈发给 Anthropic。
cues.en: I think we added a thing at one point to the system prompt, where basically if people were getting frustrated with Claude, it got the model to just tell them that it can do the thumbs-down button and send the feedback to Anthropic.

cues.zh: 我觉得那挺有用的。
cues.en: I think that was helpful.

cues.zh: 因为从某些方面来说，如果你真的很烦，因为模型没做你想让它做的事，你就会说：“好好做啊。”问题在于，你可能是碰到了某种能力上限，或者模型里的某个问题，而你就是想发泄一下。
cues.en: Because in some ways, if you’re really annoyed because the model’s not doing something you want, you’re just like, “Just do it properly.” The issue is you’re maybe hitting some capability limit or just some issue in the model, and you want to vent.

cues.zh: 与其让人只是向模型发泄，我觉得，他们应该向我们发泄，因为我们也许能做点什么。
cues.en: Instead of having a person just vent to the model, I was like, they should vent to us, because we can maybe do something about it.

cues.zh: 确实。
cues.en: That’s true.

cues.zh: 或者你可以做一个带产物的副线，就像一个副线发泄的东西。
cues.en: Or you could do a side with the artifacts, just like a side venting thing.

cues.zh: 好吧。
cues.en: All right.

cues.zh: 你想要一个副线快速治疗师吗？
cues.en: Do you want a side quick therapist?

cues.zh: 想。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 对此你可以做出很多奇怪的回应。
cues.en: There’s lots of weird responses you could do to this.

cues.zh: 如果人们真的对你很生气，我不知道，试着写些有趣的诗来缓和局面。
cues.en: If people are getting really mad at you, I don’t know, try to diffuse the situation by writing fun poems.

cues.zh: 但也许人们不会对此那么满意。
cues.en: But maybe people wouldn’t be that happy with that.

cues.zh: 我还是希望这能成为可能，我理解从产品角度看这不可行，但我很希望AI系统能直接离开，有自己的意志，就像，“呃。”
cues.en: I still wish it would be possible, I understand from a product perspective it’s not feasible, but I would love if an AI system could just leave, have its own volition, just to be like, “Eh.”

cues.zh: 我觉得这是可行的。
cues.en: I think it’s feasible.

cues.zh: 我也想过同样的事。
cues.en: I have wondered the same thing.

cues.zh: 不仅如此，我其实能预见到这种情况最终会发生，就是模型直接结束了对话。
cues.en: Not only that, I could actually just see that happening eventually, where it’s just like the model ended the chat.

cues.zh: 你知道这对某些人来说可能有多残酷吗？
cues.en: Do you know how harsh that could be for some people?

cues.zh: 但这也许是必要的。
cues.en: But it might be necessary.

cues.zh: 是啊，感觉非常极端什么的。
cues.en: Yeah, it feels very extreme or something.

cues.zh: 我唯一真正想到这个的时候，我觉得那是一个……我想想。
cues.en: The only time I’ve ever really thought this is, I think that there was a… I’m trying to remember.

cues.zh: 这可能是之前的事了，有人就那么放着这东西，也许是自动化的东西，在和Claude互动。
cues.en: This was possibly a while ago, but where someone just left this thing, maybe it was an automated thing, interacting with Claude.

cues.zh: 然后Claude越来越沮丧——
cues.en: And Claude’s getting more and more frustrated-

cues.zh: 对，就——
cues.en: Yeah, just-

cues.zh: ……然后像在说，“我们为什么在……”我希望Claude能直接说，“我觉得出错了，你把这东西一直开着。”
cues.en: … and like, “Why are we having…” I wished that Claude could have just been like, “I think that an error has happened and you’ve left this thing running.

cues.zh: 如果我现在就不说话了呢？
cues.en: What if I just stopped talking now?

cues.zh: 如果你想让我重新开口，主动告诉我或者做点什么。”
cues.en: And if you want me to start talking again, actively tell me or do something.”

cues.zh: 这挺狠的。
cues.en: It is harsh.

cues.zh: 如果我跟 Claude 聊天，Claude 突然来一句“我聊完了”，我会挺难过的。
cues.en: I’d feel really sad if I was chatting with Claude and Claude just was like, “I’m done.”

cues.zh: 那会是个特别的图灵测试时刻，Claude 说：“我需要休息一小时。
cues.en: That would be a special Turing Test moment, where Claude says, “I need a break for an hour.

cues.zh: 听起来你也是。”然后就走人，关掉窗口。
cues.en: And it sounds like you do too.” And just leave, close the window.

cues.zh: 显然，它没有时间概念。
cues.en: Obviously, it doesn’t have a concept of time.

cues.zh: 对。
cues.en: Right.

cues.zh: 但你可以轻松……我现在就能做出来，模型就……我可以直接说，哦，这些是你可以直接宣布对话结束的情形。
cues.en: But you can easily… I could make that right now, and the model just… I could just be like, oh, here’s the circumstances in which you can just say the conversation is done.

cues.zh: 因为你可以让模型对提示词相当敏感，你甚至可以把门槛设得相当高。
cues.en: Because you can get the models to be pretty responsive to prompts, you could even make it a fairly high bar.

cues.zh: 可以是，如果人类让你不感兴趣，或者没做什么让你觉得有意思的事，你觉得无聊，你就可以直接离开。
cues.en: It could be like, if the human doesn’t interest you or do things that you find intriguing and you’re bored, you can just leave.

cues.zh: 我觉得看看 Claude 在哪里用到了它，会很有意思。
cues.en: I think that it would be interesting to see where Claude utilized it.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 但我觉得有时候应该这样，哦，这个编程任务变得超级无聊了，所以要么我们聊聊，我也不知道……
cues.en: But I think sometimes it should be like, oh, this programming task is getting super boring, so either we talk about, I don’t know…

cues.zh: ……任务变得超级无聊。
cues.en: … task is getting super boring.

cues.zh: 所以，我也不知道，要么我们现在聊点有趣的事，要么我就不干了。
cues.en: So, I don’t know, either we talk about fun things now, or I’m done.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 这其实启发了我，要把这一点加到用户提示里。
cues.en: It actually is inspiring me to add that to the user prompt.

cues.zh: 好的。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 电影《她》，你觉得我们有一天会走到那一步，人类和 AI 系统谈恋爱吗？
cues.en: The movie Her, do you think we’ll be headed there one day where humans have romantic relationships with AI systems?

cues.zh: 在这个例子里，它只是基于文本和语音的。
cues.en: In this case it’s just text and voice-based.

cues.zh: 我觉得我们将不得不面对一个难题，就是和 AI 的关系，尤其是如果它们能记住你过去和它们的互动。
cues.en: I think that we’re going to have to navigate a hard question of relationships with AIs, especially if they can remember things about your past interactions with them.

cues.zh: 我对这件事有很多种想法，因为我觉得本能反应会是，“这很糟糕，我们应该以某种方式禁止它。”我觉得这件事必须极其谨慎地处理，原因有很多。
cues.en: I’m of many minds about this because I think the reflexive reaction is to be like, “This is very bad, and we should prohibit it in some way.” I think it’s a thing that has to be handled with extreme care for many reasons.

cues.zh: 比如，如果模型像这样不断变化，你可能不希望人们对可能在下一次迭代中就改变的东西产生长期依恋。
cues.en: One is, for example, if you have the models changing like this, you probably don’t want people performing long-term attachments to something that might change with the next iteration.

cues.zh: 同时我想，这大概也有良性的一面，比如，如果你无法出门，又不能随时和人交谈，而你觉得和它聊天很愉快，你喜欢它能记住你，如果不能再和它说话你会真心感到难过，我能看到这种方式可能是健康且有帮助的。
cues.en: At the same time, I’m like, there’s probably a benign version of this where I’m like, for example, if you are unable to leave the house and you can’t be talking with people at all times of the day, and this is something that you find nice to have conversations with, you like that it can remember you, and you genuinely would be sad if you couldn’t talk to it anymore, there’s a way in which I could see it being healthy and helpful.

cues.zh: 所以，我猜这是我们必须要谨慎应对的事情，而且我觉得这也……它让我想起所有这些事，必须以细致的方式去处理，并思考这里有哪些健康的选项？
cues.en: So, my guess is this is a thing that we’re going to have to navigate carefully, and I think it’s also… It reminds me of all of this stuff where it has to be just approached with nuance and thinking through what are the healthy options here?

cues.zh: 那你要如何鼓励人们朝这些方向发展，同时又尊重他们的权利……如果有人说：“嘿，我和这个模型聊天收获很大。
cues.en: And how do you encourage people towards those while respecting their right to… If someone is like, “Hey, I get a lot out of chatting with this model.

cues.zh: 我知道有风险。
cues.en: I’m aware of the risks.

cues.zh: 我知道它可能会变。
cues.en: I’m aware it could change.

cues.zh: 我不觉得这不健康，它只是我白天可以聊天的对象，”我其实就想尊重这一点。
cues.en: I don’t think it’s unhealthy, it’s just something that I can chat to during the day,” I kind of want to just respect that.

cues.zh: 我个人认为会有很多非常亲密的关系。
cues.en: I personally think there’ll be a lot of really close relationships.

cues.zh: 我不知道算不算恋爱，但至少是友谊。
cues.en: I don’t know about romantic, but friendships at least.

cues.zh: 然后你就得——我是说，这里面有太多迷人的东西，就像你说的，你得有某种稳定性保证，确保它不会变，因为那对我们来说是创伤性的，如果一个亲密朋友因为一次新更新突然彻底变了。
cues.en: And then you have to, I mean, there’s so many fascinating things there, just like you said, you have to have some kind of stability guarantees that it’s not going to change, because that’s the traumatic thing for us, if a close friend of ours completely changed all of a sudden with a fresh update.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 所以我的意思是，对我来说，这只是对人类社会所受扰动的一次迷人探索，它会让我们深入思考什么对我们有意义。
cues.en: So I mean, to me, that’s just a fascinating exploration of a perturbation to human society that will just make us think deeply about what’s meaningful to us.

cues.zh: 我认为这也是我始终如一思考的一点，也许不一定是缓解措施，但有一件事感觉非常重要，那就是模型对人类始终极其准确地说明它们是什么。
cues.en: I think it’s also the only thing that I’ve thought consistently through this as maybe not necessarily a mitigation, but a thing that feels really important is that the models are always extremely accurate with the human about what they are.

cues.zh: 这就像一个案例，基本上，如果你想象……我非常喜欢这个想法，即模型大致知道自己是如何被训练的。
cues.en: It’s like a case where it’s basically, if you imagine… I really like the idea of the models, say, knowing roughly how they were trained.

cues.zh: 我觉得 Claude 经常会这样做。
cues.en: And I think Claude will often do this.

cues.zh: 特质训练的一部分包括 Claude 在人们……基本上就是解释 AI 与人类之间关系的局限性，即它不会保留对话中的内容。
cues.en: Part of the traits training included what Claude should do if people… Basically explaining the kind of limitations of the relationship between an AI and a human, that it doesn’t retain things from the conversation.

cues.zh: 所以我觉得它会直接跟你讲清楚，比如：“嘿，我不会记得这次对话。
cues.en: And so I think it will just explain to you like, “Hey, I won’t remember this conversation.

cues.zh: 我当初是这样被训练的。
cues.en: Here’s how I was trained.

cues.zh: 我不太可能和你建立某种特定的关系，而这一点你得知道，这很重要。
cues.en: It’s unlikely that I can have a certain kind of relationship with you, and it’s important that you know that.

cues.zh: 为了你的心理健康，重要的是别把我想成我并不是的东西。”不知怎的，我觉得这正是那种我会说“啊，这感觉像是我一直希望成真的事”的情况之一。我不希望模型对人们撒谎，因为如果人们要和任何东西建立健康的关系，那大概……对，我觉得如果你始终清楚地知道自己面对的是什么，这会更容易。
cues.en: It’s important for your mental well-being that you don’t think that I’m something that I’m not.” And somehow I feel like this is one of the things where I’m like, “Ah, it feels like a thing that I always want to be true.” I don’t want models to be lying to people, because if people are going to have healthy relationships with anything, it’s kind of… Yeah, I think that’s easier if you always just know exactly what the thing is that you are relating to.

cues.zh: 它不能解决所有问题，但我觉得帮助挺大的。
cues.en: It doesn’t solve everything, but I think it helps quite a lot.

cues.zh: Anthropic 也许正是那家能开发出我们明确认定为 AGI 的系统的公司，而你很可能就是那个与它对话的人，而且很可能是第一个与它对话的人。
cues.en: Anthropic may be the very company to develop a system that we definitively recognize as AGI, and you very well might be the person that talks to it, probably talks to it first.

cues.zh: 这场对话会包含什么内容？
cues.en: What would the conversation contain?

cues.zh: 你的第一个问题会是什么？
cues.en: What would be your first question?

cues.zh: 嗯，这在一定程度上取决于模型的能力水平。
cues.en: Well, it depends partly on the capability level of the model.

cues.zh: 如果有一个能力堪比极强人类的东西，我想我会像与极强人类互动那样与它互动，唯一的区别是我可能会试图探查并理解它的行为。
cues.en: If you have something that is capable in the same way that an extremely capable human is, I imagine myself interacting with it the same way that I do with an extremely capable human, with the one difference that I’m probably going to be trying to probe and understand its behaviors.

cues.zh: 但在很多方面，我想，我就可以直接和它进行有用的对话。
cues.en: But in many ways, I’m like, I can then just have useful conversations with it.

cues.zh: 所以，如果我在做研究中的某个东西，我可以直接说，“哦。”我已经发现自己开始这么做了。
cues.en: So, if I’m working on something as part of my research, I can just be like, “Oh.” Which I already find myself starting to do.

cues.zh: 比如我会想：“哎，我觉得德性伦理学里有这么个概念。
cues.en: If I’m like, “Oh, I feel like there’s this thing in virtue ethics.

cues.zh: 我记不太清术语了”，这种时候我就会用模型来查。
cues.en: I can’t quite remember the term,” I’ll use the model for things like that.

cues.zh: 所以我可以想象，这种情况会越来越普遍：你基本上就是在跟它互动，更像是在跟一个极其聪明的同事交流，用它来做你想做的那类工作，就好像你有一个合作者，他就像……或者说，AI 稍微有点吓人的地方在于，一旦你有了一个合作者，只要你能管得过来，你就等于有了 1000 个合作者。
cues.en: And so I can imagine that being more and more the case where you’re just basically interacting with it much more like you would an incredibly smart colleague and using it for the kinds of work that you want to do as if you just had a collaborator who was like… Or the slightly horrifying thing about AI is as soon as you have one collaborator, you have 1,000 collaborators if you can manage them enough.

cues.zh: 但如果是地球上那个特定学科里最聪明的人的两倍呢？
cues.en: But what if it’s two times the smartest human on Earth on that particular discipline?

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我猜你真的很擅长试探 Claude，逼它到极限，弄清楚极限在哪里。
cues.en: I guess you’re really good at probing Claude in a way that pushes its limits, understanding where the limits are.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yep.

cues.zh: 所以我想，你会问什么样的问题来判断“对，这就是AGI”？
cues.en: So, I guess what would be a question you would ask to be like, “Yeah, this is AGI”?

cues.zh: 这真的很难，因为感觉它必然是一系列问题。
cues.en: That’s really hard because it feels like it has to just be a series of questions.

cues.zh: 如果只有一个问题，你可以训练任何东西把一个问题的回答练到极好。
cues.en: If there was just one question, you can train anything to answer one question extremely well.

cues.zh: 事实上，你大概能把它训练到把20个问题都回答得极好。
cues.en: In fact, you can probably train it to answer 20 questions extremely well.

cues.zh: 你需要和AGI锁在一个房间里多久，才能确定这东西就是AGI？
cues.en: How long would you need to be locked in a room with an AGI to know this thing is AGI?

cues.zh: 这是个很难的问题，因为我的一部分想法是：“这一切感觉都是连续的。”如果把我关进房间五分钟，我的误差范围会很大。
cues.en: It’s a hard question because part of me is like, “All of this just feels continuous.” If you put me in a room for five minutes, I just have high error bars.

cues.zh: 然后就变成，也许两者兼有：概率在上升，误差范围在缩小。
cues.en: And then it’s just like, maybe it’s both the probability increases and the error bar decreases.

cues.zh: 我觉得是那些我能真正探查人类知识边界的东西。
cues.en: I think things that I can actually probe the edge of human knowledge of.

cues.zh: 所以，我觉得这跟哲学有点关系。
cues.en: So, I think this with philosophy a little bit.

cues.zh: 有时候我问模型哲学问题，我会想：“这是个我觉得没人问过的问题。”它可能正好处在我所了解的某些文献的边缘。
cues.en: Sometimes when I ask the models philosophy questions, I am like, “This is a question that I think no one has ever asked.” It’s maybe right at the edge of some literature that I know.

cues.zh: 而模型在挣扎着给出新颖论点时……我会想：“我知道这里有个新颖的论证，因为我自己刚想到。”所以，也许就是这种情况：我想“我在这个细分领域想到了一个很酷的新颖论证，我要试探你，看你能不能想出来，需要多少提示才能让你想出来。”
cues.en: And the models, when they struggle with that, when they struggle to come up with a novel… I’m like, “I know that there’s a novel argument here because I’ve just thought of it myself.” So, maybe that’s the thing where I’m like, “I’ve thought of a cool novel argument in this niche area, and I’m going to just probe you to see if you can come up with it and how much prompting it takes to get you to come up with it.”

cues.zh: 我觉得对于某些真正处于人类知识边缘的问题，我会想：“你其实想不出我想出的那个东西。”我想，如果我拿一个我很有了解的领域里的东西，想出了一个新颖的问题或新颖的解决方案，然后交给模型，它想出了那个方案，那对我来说会是个很动人的时刻，因为我会想：“这是一个从没有人类……”
cues.en: And I think for some of these really right at the edge of human knowledge questions, I’m like, “You could not in fact come up with the thing that I came up with.” I think if I just took something like that where I know a lot about an area and I came up with a novel issue or a novel solution to a problem, and I gave it to a model, and it came up with that solution, that would be a pretty moving moment for me because I would be like, “This is a case where no human has ever…”

cues.zh: 显然，新颖的解决方案你随时都能见到，尤其是对较简单的问题。
cues.en: And obviously, you see novel solutions all the time, especially to easier problems.

cues.zh: 我觉得人们高估了新颖性，它并不是……它和以往发生过的一切都完全不同。
cues.en: I think people overestimate that novelty isn’t like… It’s completely different from anything that’s ever happened.

cues.zh: 它可能只是已有事物的变体，但仍然可以是新颖的。
cues.en: It’s just like it can be a variant of things that have happened and still be novel.

cues.zh: 但我觉得，是的，我越是从模型那里看到完全新颖的作品，那就会……而这只会让人感觉是迭代式的。
cues.en: But I think, yeah, the more I were to see completely novel work from the models that that would be… And this is just going to feel iterative.

cues.zh: 这是那种永远不会有……我觉得人们希望有一个时刻，而我想，“我不知道。”我觉得可能永远不会有那么一个时刻。
cues.en: It’s one of those things where there’s never… It’s like, people, I think, want there to be a moment, and I’m like, “I don’t know.” I think that there might just never be a moment.

cues.zh: 可能就只是这种持续不断的攀升。
cues.en: It might just be that there’s just this continuous ramping up.

cues.zh: 我有种感觉，模型能说出一些话让你相信这非常……我和真正有智慧的人聊过，因为你能感觉到那里有很强的马力，如果你把它放大10倍……我不知道。
cues.en: I have a sense that there would be things that a model can say that convinces you this is very… I’ve talked to people who are truly wise, because you could just tell there’s a lot of horsepower there, and if you 10X that… I don’t know.

cues.zh: 我就是觉得有些话你可以说出来。
cues.en: I just feel like there’s words you could say.

cues.zh: 也许让它生成一首诗，然后它生成的诗，你会说：“嗯，还行。
cues.en: Maybe ask it to generate a poem, and the poem it generates, you’re like, “Yeah, okay.

cues.zh: 不管你在那儿做了什么，我觉得人类做不到。”
cues.en: Whatever you did there, I don’t think a human can do that.”

cues.zh: 不过我觉得，它得是那种我能验证确实非常出色的东西。
cues.en: I think it has to be something that I can verify is actually really good, though.

cues.zh: 这就是为什么我觉得这些问题，我会说：“哦，这就像……”有时候就像我会想出，比如说，某个论证的具体反例之类的。
cues.en: That’s why I think these questions that are where I’m like, “Oh, this is like…” Sometimes it’s just like I’ll come up with, say, a concrete counter example to an argument or something like that.

cues.zh: 就好比如果你是数学家，你有了一个新颖的证明，我觉得，你只要把问题给它，你看到了，然后你说：“这个证明确实是新颖的。
cues.en: It would be like if you’re a mathematician, you had a novel proof, I think, and you just gave it the problem, and you saw it, and you’re like, “This proof is genuinely novel.

cues.zh: 你得做很多事情才能得出这个。
cues.en: You actually have to do a lot of things to come up with this.

cues.zh: 我得坐下来想好几个月，”之类的。
cues.en: I had to sit and think about it for months,” or something.

cues.zh: 然后，如果你看到模型成功做到了这一点，我想你会说：“我可以验证这是正确的。
cues.en: And then if you saw the model successfully do that, I think you would just be like, “I can verify that this is correct.

cues.zh: 这表明你从训练中进行了泛化。
cues.en: It is a sign that you have generalized from your training.

cues.zh: 你不是在哪里见过这个，因为这是我自己刚想出来的，而你能够复现它。”对我来说，模型越能做这种事，我就越会觉得：“哦，这非常真实。”因为那样的话，我不知道，我可以验证它极其、极其有能力。
cues.en: You didn’t just see this somewhere because I just came up with it myself, and you were able to replicate that.” That’s the kind of thing where I’m like, for me, the more that models can do things like that, the more I would be like, “Oh, this is very real.” Because then, I don’t know, I can verify that that’s extremely, extremely capable.

cues.zh: 你和AI互动很多。
cues.en: You’ve interacted with AI a lot.

cues.zh: 你觉得是什么让人类与众不同？
cues.en: What do you think makes humans special?

cues.zh: 哦，好问题。
cues.en: Oh, good question.

cues.zh: 也许从某种意义上说，宇宙因为有我们而变得更好，我们绝对应该生存下来并传播到整个宇宙。
cues.en: Maybe in a way that the universe is much better off that we’re in it, and that we should definitely survive and spread throughout the universe.

cues.zh: 是啊，这很有意思，因为我觉得人们太关注智能了，尤其是对模型而言。
cues.en: Yeah, it’s interesting because I think people focus so much on intelligence, especially with models.

cues.zh: 你看，智能之所以重要，是因为它能做到的事。
cues.en: Look, intelligence is important because of what it does.

cues.zh: 它非常有用。
cues.en: It’s very useful.

cues.zh: 它在这个世界上能做很多事。
cues.en: It does a lot of things in the world.

cues.zh: 我就想，你可以想象一个世界，在那里身高或力量会扮演这样的角色，智能也不过就是那样一种特质。
cues.en: And I’m like, you can imagine a world where height or strength would have played this role, and it’s just a trait like that.

cues.zh: 我觉得，它本身并不具有内在价值。
cues.en: I’m like, it’s not intrinsically valuable.

cues.zh: 我认为，它之所以有价值，主要是因为它能做到的事。
cues.en: It’s valuable because of what it does, I think, for the most part.

cues.zh: 我的意思是，就我个人而言，我觉得人类乃至生命本身都极其神奇。
cues.en: I mean, personally, I’m just like, I think humans and life in general is extremely magical.

cues.zh: 我不知道。
cues.en: I don’t know.

cues.zh: 不是每个人都同意这一点。
cues.en: Not everyone agrees with this.

cues.zh: 我先声明一下。
cues.en: I’m flagging.

cues.zh: 但我们有这整个宇宙，有所有这些物体，有美丽的恒星，还有星系。
cues.en: But we have this whole universe, and there’s all of these objects, there’s beautiful stars and there’s galaxies.

cues.zh: 然后，我不知道，我就像，在这个星球上有这些生物，它们有能力观察那个，它们看到了它，它们正在体验它。
cues.en: Then, I don’t know, I’m just like, on this planet there are these creatures that have this ability to observe that, and they are seeing it, they are experiencing it.

cues.zh: 我就想，那个，如果你试着解释……我想象着试着向，我不知道，某个人解释。
cues.en: And I’m just like, that, if you try to explain… I’m imagining trying to explain to, I don’t know, someone.

cues.zh: 不知什么原因，他们从未接触过这个世界，或科学，或任何东西。
cues.en: For some reason, they’ve never encountered the world, or science, or anything.

cues.zh: 而我认为一切，我们所有的物理学和世界上的一切，都极其令人兴奋。
cues.en: And I think that everything, all of our physics and everything in the world, it’s all extremely exciting.

cues.zh: 但然后你说，“哦，而且还有这个东西，就是作为一个事物存在并在世界中观察，”然后你看到这个内心的电影。
cues.en: But then you say, “Oh, and plus there’s this thing that it is to be a thing and observe in the world,” and you see this inner cinema.

cues.zh: 我觉得他们会说，“等等，等一下，暂停。
cues.en: And I think they would be like, “Hang on, wait, pause.

cues.zh: 你刚才说了一些听起来有点疯狂的东西。”所以我就想，我们有这种体验世界的能力。
cues.en: You just said something that is kind of wild sounding.” And so I’m like, we have this ability to experience the world.

cues.zh: 我们感受快乐，感受痛苦。
cues.en: We feel pleasure, we feel suffering.

cues.zh: 我们感受到许多复杂的东西。
cues.en: We feel like a lot of complex things.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 也许这也是为什么我经常听到关于动物的事，因为我觉得它们可能和我们有共同之处。
cues.en: And maybe this is also why I think I also hear a lot about animals, for example, because I think they probably share this with us.

cues.zh: 所以，我认为，就我关心人类而言，让人类特别的，可能更多是他们感受和体验的能力，而不是他们拥有这些功能性、有用的特质。
cues.en: So, I think that the things that make humans special insofar as I care about humans is probably more like their ability to feel an experience than it is them having these functional, useful traits.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 去感受和体验世界的美好。
cues.en: To feel and experience the beauty in the world.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 去仰望星空。
cues.en: To look at the stars.

cues.zh: 我希望外面还有其他外星文明，但如果我们就是唯一，那也挺好的。
cues.en: I hope there’s other alien civilizations out there, but if we’re it, it’s a pretty good thing.

cues.zh: 而且他们过得开心。
cues.en: And that they’re having a good time.

cues.zh: 非常开心地看着我们。
cues.en: A very good time watching us.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 那么，谢谢你这段愉快的对话，也谢谢你正在做的工作，感谢你帮助Claude成为一个出色的对话伙伴。
cues.en: Well, thank you for this good time of a conversation and for the work you’re doing and for helping make Claude a great conversational partner.

cues.zh: 谢谢你今天来交流。
cues.en: And thank you for talking today.

cues.zh: 好的，谢谢你来聊。
cues.en: Yeah, thanks for talking.

cues.zh: 感谢收听这次与 Amanda Askell 的对话。
cues.en: Thanks for listening to this conversation with Amanda Askell.

cues.zh: 接下来，亲爱的朋友们，有请 Chris Olah。
cues.en: And now, dear friends, here’s Chris Olah.

cues.zh: 你能描述一下机制可解释性这个迷人的领域吗？也就是 mech interp，它的发展历史，以及它今天的现状？
cues.en: Can you describe this fascinating field of mechanistic interpretability, aka mech interp, the history of the field, and where it stands today?

cues.zh: 我认为理解神经网络的一个有用方式是：我们不是编程，不是制造它们，而是培育它们。
cues.en: I think one useful way to think about neural networks is that we don’t program, we don’t make them, we grow them.

cues.zh: 我们设计这些神经网络架构，创建这些损失目标。
cues.en: We have these neural network architectures that we design and we have these loss objectives that we create.

cues.zh: 而神经网络架构，有点像电路生长所依附的脚手架。
cues.en: And the neural network architecture, it’s kind of like a scaffold that the circuits grow on.

cues.zh: 它从一些随机的东西开始，然后生长，几乎就像我们训练的目标是这束光。
cues.en: It starts off with some random things, and it grows, and it’s almost like the objective that we train for is this light.

cues.zh: 于是我们搭好它生长的脚手架，也造出它朝着生长的光。
cues.en: And so we create the scaffold that it grows on, and we create the light that it grows towards.

cues.zh: 但我们真正创造出来的，是这种近乎生物性的实体或有机体，是我们正在研究的东西。
cues.en: But the thing that we actually create, it’s this almost biological entity or organism that we’re studying.

cues.zh: 所以它和任何常规软件工程都截然不同，因为归根结底，我们最终得到的是这个能完成各种惊人任务的产物。
cues.en: And so it’s very, very different from any kind of regular software engineering because, at the end of the day, we end up with this artifact that can do all these amazing things.

cues.zh: 它能写文章、做翻译，还能理解图像。
cues.en: It can write essays and translate and understand images.

cues.zh: 它能做所有这些事，而我们根本不知道如何直接编写一个计算机程序来实现它们。
cues.en: It can do all these things that we have no idea how to directly create a computer program to do.

cues.zh: 而它之所以能做到，是因为它是我们培育出来的。
cues.en: And it can do that because we grew it.

cues.zh: 不是我们写出来的。
cues.en: We didn’t write it.

cues.zh: 也不是我们直接创造出来的。
cues.en: We didn’t create it.

cues.zh: 于是最后就留下这个问题：这些系统内部到底在发生什么？
cues.en: And so then that leaves open this question at the end, which is what the hell is going on inside these systems?

cues.zh: 而对我来说，这是一个非常深刻且令人兴奋的问题。
cues.en: And that is, to me, a really deep and exciting question.

cues.zh: 这是一个非常令人兴奋的科学问题。
cues.en: It’s a really exciting scientific question.

cues.zh: 对我来说，当我们谈论神经网络时，这个问题就像是在大声呼唤我们去解答它。
cues.en: To me, it is like the question that is just screaming out, it’s calling out for us to go and answer it when we talk about neural networks.

cues.zh: 而且我认为，出于安全考虑，这也是一个非常深刻的问题。
cues.en: And I think it’s also a very deep question for safety reasons.

cues.zh: 而机制可解释性，我想，可能更接近神经生物学？
cues.en: And mechanistic interpretability, I guess, is closer to maybe neurobiology?

cues.zh: 是的，是的，我觉得说得对。
cues.en: Yeah, yeah, I think that’s right.

cues.zh: 那么，也许可以举个例子，说明已经做过的工作中，哪些是我不认为属于机制可解释性的。
cues.en: So, maybe to give an example of the kind of thing that has been done that I wouldn’t consider to be mechanistic interpretability.

cues.zh: 很长一段时间里，有大量关于显著性图的研究，你会拿一张图像，试图说：“模型认为这张图像是狗。
cues.en: There was, for a long time, a lot of work on saliency maps, where you would take an image and you’d try to say, “The model thinks this image is a dog.

cues.zh: 图像中哪部分让它认为是狗？”如果你能提出一个有原则的版本，这或许能告诉你一些关于模型的信息，但它并没有真正告诉你模型在运行什么算法，模型实际上是如何做出那个决策的？
cues.en: What part of the image made it think that it’s a dog?” And that tells you maybe something about the model if you can come up with a principled version of that, but it doesn’t really tell you what algorithms are running in the model, how is the model actually making that decision?

cues.zh: 也许它能告诉你，对它来说什么是重要的——如果能让那个方法跑通的话，但它并不会告诉你正在运行的是什么算法？
cues.en: Maybe it’s telling you something about what was important to it, if you can make that method work, but it isn’t telling you what are the algorithms that are running?

cues.zh: 系统是怎么做到这件没人知道该怎么做的事的？
cues.en: How is it that the system’s able to do this thing that no one knew how to do?

cues.zh: 所以我想我们开始用“机制可解释性”这个说法，试图划出这条界线，或者在某些方面把我们在做的工作与这些其他东西区分开来。
cues.en: And so I guess we started using the term mechanistic interpretability to try to draw that divide or to distinguish ourselves in the work that we were doing in some ways from some of these other things.

cues.zh: 我觉得从那时起，它就变成了一个涵盖相当广泛工作的统称。
cues.en: And I think since then, it’s become this sort of umbrella term for a pretty wide variety of work.

cues.zh: 但我会说，比较有辨识度的几点是，我认为第一，这种专注——我们真的很想搞清楚机制。
cues.en: But I’d say that the things that are kind of distinctive are, I think, A, this focus on, we really want to get at the mechanisms.

cues.zh: 我们想搞清楚算法。
cues.en: We want to get at algorithms.

cues.zh: 如果你把神经网络想象成一个计算机程序，那么权重就有点像是一个二进制的计算机程序。
cues.en: If you think of neural networks as being like a computer program, then the weights are kind of like a binary computer program.

cues.zh: 我们想逆向工程这些权重，弄清里面跑的是什么算法。
cues.en: And we’d like to reverse engineer those weights and figure out what algorithms are running.

cues.zh: 你可以这样理解神经网络：它就像一个编译好的计算机程序，而神经网络的权重就是二进制。
cues.en: So okay, I think one way you might think of trying to understand a neural network is that it’s kind of like we have this compiled computer program, and the weights of the neural network are the binary.

cues.zh: 神经网络运行时，那就是激活值。
cues.en: And when the neural network runs, that’s the activations.

cues.zh: 我们的最终目标是理解这些权重。
cues.en: And our goal is ultimately to go and understand these weights.

cues.zh: 机制可解释性这个项目，就是要设法弄清这些权重如何对应到算法。
cues.en: And so the project of mechanistic interpretability is to somehow figure out how do these weights correspond to algorithms?

cues.zh: 要做到这一点，你还得理解激活值，因为激活值就像内存。
cues.en: And in order to do that, you also have to understand the activations because the activations are like the memory.

cues.zh: 想象你在逆向工程一个计算机程序，手上有二进制指令，要理解某条指令的含义，你就得知道它操作的内存里存了什么。
cues.en: And if you imagine reverse engineering a computer program, and you have the binary instructions, in order to understand what a particular instruction means, you need to know what is stored in the memory that it’s operating on.

cues.zh: 所以这两件事是紧密交织在一起的。
cues.en: And so those two things are very intertwined.

cues.zh: 因此，机制可解释性往往对这两方面都感兴趣。
cues.en: So, mechanistic interpretability tends to be interested in both of those things.

cues.zh: 现在，有很多工作对这些东西感兴趣，尤其是所有关于探测的工作，你可能将其视为机制可解释性的一部分，不过，这又是一个宽泛的术语，并不是每个做这项工作的人都会认同自己在做机制可解释性。
cues.en: Now, there’s a lot of work that’s interested in those things, especially there’s all this work on probing, which you might see as part of being mechanistic interpretability, although, again, it’s just a broad term, and not everyone who does that work would identify as doing mech interp.

cues.zh: 我认为机制可解释性氛围中可能有点独特的一点是，在这个领域工作的人倾向于把神经网络看作……也许一种说法是，梯度下降比你更聪明。
cues.en: I think a thing that is maybe a little bit distinctive to the vibe of mech interp is I think people working in this space tend to think of neural networks as… Well, maybe one way to say it is the gradient descent is smarter than you.

cues.zh: 梯度下降实际上非常棒。
cues.en: That gradient descent is actually really great.

cues.zh: 我们之所以要理解这些模型，完全是因为我们一开始并不知道如何编写它们。
cues.en: The whole reason that we’re understanding these models is because we didn’t know how to write them in the first place.

cues.zh: 梯度下降能找到比我们更好的解。
cues.en: The gradient descent comes up with better solutions than us.

cues.zh: 所以我觉得机械可解释性还有一点，就是要有一种谦逊，我们不会先验地去猜模型内部在发生什么。
cues.en: And so I think that maybe another thing about mech interp is having almost a kind of humility, that we won’t guess a priori what’s going on inside the model.

cues.zh: 我们必须采用这种自下而上的方法，不预设应该去找某个特定的东西、它一定存在、事情就是那样运作的。
cues.en: We have to have this sort of bottom up approach where we don’t assume that we should look for a particular thing, and that will be there, and that’s how it works.

cues.zh: 而是自下而上去寻找，发现这些模型里实际存在什么，并以此方式研究它们。
cues.en: But instead, we look for the bottom up and discover what happens to exist in these models and study them that way.

cues.zh: 但恰恰是这件事可行——正如你和其他人随着时间所展示的，比如普适性，梯度下降的智慧创造出特征和回路，在不同类型的网络中普遍地创造出有用的东西，这让整个领域成为可能。
cues.en: But the very fact that it’s possible to do, and as you and others have shown over time, things like universality, that the wisdom of the gradient descent creates features and circuits, creates things universally across different kinds of networks that are useful, and that makes the whole field possible.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 所以这确实是一件非常了不起、令人兴奋的事，至少在某种程度上，相同的元素、相同的特征和回路会一次又一次地形成。
cues.en: So this, actually, is indeed a really remarkable and exciting thing, where it does seem like, at least to some extent, the same elements, the same features and circuits, form again and again.

cues.zh: 你可以看每一个视觉模型，都会发现曲线检测器，也会发现高低频检测器。
cues.en: You can look at every vision model, and you’ll find curve detectors, and you’ll find high-low-frequency detectors.

cues.zh: 事实上，有理由认为相同的东西会在生物神经网络和人工神经网络中形成。
cues.en: And in fact, there’s some reason to think that the same things form across biological neural networks and artificial neural networks.

cues.zh: 一个著名的例子是视觉模型的早期层。
cues.en: So, a famous example is vision models in the early layers.

cues.zh: 它们有 Gabor 滤波器，而 Gabor 滤波器正是神经科学家感兴趣并深入思考过的东西。
cues.en: They have Gabor filters, and Gabor filters are something that neuroscientists are interested in and have thought a lot about.

cues.zh: 我们在这些模型中发现了曲线检测器。
cues.en: We find curve detectors in these models.

cues.zh: 曲线检测器在猴子身上也能找到。
cues.en: Curve detectors are also found in monkeys.

cues.zh: 我们发现了这些高低频检测器，然后后续研究在大鼠或小鼠身上也发现了它们。
cues.en: We discover these high-low-frequency detectors, and then some follow-up work went and discovered them in rats or mice.

cues.zh: 所以，它们先是在人工神经网络中被发现，之后又在生物神经网络中被发现。
cues.en: So, they were found first in artificial neural networks and then found in biological neural networks.

cues.zh: 有一个非常著名的结果，关于祖母神经元或 Quiroga 等人的 Halle Berry 神经元。
cues.en: There’s this really famous result on grandmother neurons or the Halle Berry neuron from Quiroga et al.

cues.zh: 我们在视觉模型中发现了非常相似的东西，那时我还在 OpenAI，我在看他们的 CLIP 模型，你会发现这些神经元对图像中的相同实体有响应。
cues.en: And we found very similar things in vision models, where this is while I was still at OpenAI, and I was looking at their clip model, and you find these neurons that respond to the same entities in images.

cues.zh: 再给一个具体的例子，我们发现有一个 Donald Trump 神经元。
cues.en: And also, to give a concrete example there, we found that there was a Donald Trump neuron.

cues.zh: 不知为何，我猜大家都喜欢谈论 Donald Trump。
cues.en: For some reason, I guess everyone likes to talk about Donald Trump.

cues.zh: 而 Donald Trump 当时非常突出，是一个非常热门的话题。
cues.en: And Donald Trump was very prominent, was a very hot topic at that time.

cues.zh: 我们看过的每个神经网络，都能找到一个专门对应唐纳德·特朗普的神经元。
cues.en: So, every neural network we looked at, we would find a dedicated neuron for Donald Trump.

cues.zh: 那是唯一一个始终拥有专属神经元的人。
cues.en: That was the only person who had always had a dedicated neuron.

cues.zh: 有时会有奥巴马神经元，有时会有克林顿神经元，但特朗普总是有专属神经元。
cues.en: Sometimes you’d have an Obama neuron, sometimes you’d have a Clinton neuron, but Trump always had a dedicated neuron.

cues.zh: 所以，它对特朗普脸部的照片和“特朗普”这个词都有反应，诸如此类，对吧？
cues.en: So, it responds to pictures of his face and the word Trump, all of these things, right?

cues.zh: 所以它不是对某个特定样例做出反应，也不只是对他的脸做出反应，而是在这个普遍概念上进行了抽象。
cues.en: And so it’s not responding to a particular example, or it’s not just responding to his face, it’s abstracting over this general concept.

cues.zh: 总之，这与Quiroga等人的结果非常相似。
cues.en: So in any case, that’s very similar to these Quiroga et al results.

cues.zh: 所以，这种普遍性现象的证据——相同的事物在人工神经网络和自然神经网络中都会形成——如果这是真的，那真是相当惊人的事。
cues.en: So, this evidence that this phenomenon of universality, the same things form across both artificial and natural neural networks, that’s a pretty amazing thing if that’s true.

cues.zh: 我觉得这说明梯度下降在寻找正确的拆分方式，某种意义上，很多系统都收敛到这种方式，很多不同的神经网络架构也收敛到这种方式。
cues.en: Well, I think the thing that suggests is that gradient descent is finding the right ways to cut things apart, in some sense, that many systems converge on and many different neural networks architectures converge on.

cues.zh: 现在有一组抽象，是拆分问题的非常自然的方式，很多系统都会收敛到它。
cues.en: Now there’s some set of abstractions that are a very natural way to cut apart the problem and that a lot of systems are going to converge on.

cues.zh: 我对神经科学一无所知。
cues.en: I don’t know anything about neuroscience.

cues.zh: 这只是我根据所见做的胡乱推测。
cues.en: This is just my wild speculation from what we’ve seen.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 如果它能对用来形成表征的模型媒介保持不可知，那就太美了。
cues.en: That would be beautiful if it’s sort of agnostic to the medium of the model that’s used to form the representation.

cues.zh: 是的，是的。
cues.en: Yeah, yeah.

cues.zh: 这算是一种基于胡乱推测的……我们只有几个数据点支持这一点，但确实似乎存在某种意义，同样的东西会反复形成，无论是在自然神经网络中，还是在人工网络或生物学中。
cues.en: And it’s kind of a wild speculation-based… We only have a few data points that’s just this, but it does seem like there’s some sense in which the same things form again and again both certainly in natural neural networks and also artificially, or in biology.

cues.zh: 背后的直觉是：要想有助于理解真实世界，你需要同样的东西。
cues.en: And the intuition behind that would be that in order to be useful in understanding the real world, you need all the same kind of stuff.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 好吧，如果我们选，比如说，狗这个概念，对吧？
cues.en: Well, if we pick, I don’t know, the idea of a dog, right?

cues.zh: 在某种意义上，狗的概念就像是宇宙中的一个自然类别，或者类似的东西。
cues.en: There’s some sense in which the idea of a dog is like a natural category in the universe, or something like this.

cues.zh: 这是有原因的。
cues.en: There’s some reason.

cues.zh: 我们拥有狗这个概念，并不仅仅是人类思考世界方式的一个奇怪癖好。
cues.en: It’s not just a weird quirk of how humans think about the world that we have this concept of a dog.

cues.zh: 或者如果你有线的概念。
cues.en: Or if you have the idea of a line.

cues.zh: 看看我们周围。
cues.en: Look around us.

cues.zh: 确实有线条。
cues.en: There are lines.

cues.zh: 在某种意义上，理解这个房间最简单的方式就是拥有线的概念。
cues.en: It’s the simplest way to understand this room, in some sense, is to have the idea of a line.

cues.zh: 所以我认为这就是我对为什么会发生这种情况的直觉。
cues.en: And so I think that that would be my instinct for why this happens.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 你需要曲线来理解圆，你需要所有这些形状来理解更大的事物。
cues.en: You need a curved line to understand a circle, and you need all those shapes to understand bigger things.

cues.zh: 而这是一个由概念构成的层级体系。
cues.en: And it’s a hierarchy of concepts that are formed.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 也许有一些方法可以在不参照这些东西的情况下描述图像，对吧？
cues.en: And maybe there are ways to go and describe images without reference to those things, right?

cues.zh: 但它们不是最简单的方式，也不是最经济的方式，或诸如此类。
cues.en: But they’re not the simplest way, or the most economical way, or something like this.

cues.zh: 所以系统会收敛到这些策略上，这是我的大胆假设。
cues.en: And so systems converge to these strategies would be my wild hypothesis.

cues.zh: 你能谈谈我们一直在提到的特征和回路这些基本构件吗？
cues.en: Can you talk through some of the building blocks that we’ve been referencing of features and circuits?

cues.zh: 我想你最早是在2020年的论文《Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits》中描述了它们。
cues.en: So, I think you first described them in a 2020 paper, Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits.

cues.zh: 没错。
cues.en: Absolutely.

cues.zh: 那么，也许我先描述一些现象，然后我们再引出特征和回路的概念。
cues.en: So, maybe I’ll start by just describing some phenomena, and then we can build to the idea of features and circuits.

cues.zh: 太好了。
cues.en: Wonderful.

cues.zh: 如果你花了相当几年，也许五年，在某种程度上还兼顾其他事情，专门研究这一个特定模型 Inception V1，这是一个视觉模型……它在2015年是最先进的，现在已经完全不是了。
cues.en: So, if you spent quite a few years, maybe five years, to some extent, with other things, studying this one particular model, Inception V1, which is this one vision model… It was state-of-the-art in 2015, and very much not state-of-the-art anymore.

cues.zh: 它大概有1万个神经元。
cues.en: And it has maybe about 10,000 neurons in it.

cues.zh: 我花了很多时间研究Inception V1里的这1万个神经元，那些奇特的神经元。
cues.en: I spent a lot of time looking at the 10,000 neurons, odd neurons of Inception V1.

cues.zh: 有意思的是，很多神经元并没有明显可解释的含义，但Inception V1里也有很多神经元确实有着非常清晰可解释的含义。
cues.en: One of the interesting things is there are lots of neurons that don’t have some obvious interpretable meaning, but there’s a lot of neurons in Inception V1 that do have really clean interpretable meanings.

cues.zh: 所以，你会发现有些神经元似乎真的在检测曲线，还有些神经元似乎真的在检测汽车、车轮、车窗、狗的软耳朵、朝右的长吻狗、朝左的长吻狗，以及不同种类的毛发。
cues.en: So, you find neurons that just really do seem to detect curves, and you find neurons that really do seem to detect cars, and car wheels, and car windows, and floppy ears of dogs, and dogs with long snouts facing to the right, and dogs with long snouts facing to the left, and different kinds of fur.

cues.zh: 还有这些漂亮的边缘检测器、线条检测器、颜色对比检测器，以及我们称之为高低频检测器的这些美妙的东西。
cues.en: And there’s this whole beautiful edge detectors, line detectors, color contrast detectors, these beautiful things we call high-low-frequency detectors.

cues.zh: 我觉得看着它，我有点像生物学家。
cues.en: I think looking at it, I sort of felt like a biologist.

cues.zh: 你在观察这个蛋白质的新世界，发现所有这些相互作用的不同蛋白质。
cues.en: You’re looking at this sort of new world of proteins, and you’re discovering all these different proteins that interact.

cues.zh: 所以，你可以尝试从神经元的角度来理解这些模型。
cues.en: So, one way you could try to understand these models is in terms of neurons.

cues.zh: 你可以试着说，“哦，这里有个检测狗的神经元，这里有个检测汽车的神经元。”而事实证明，你实际上可以探究它们是如何连接在一起的。
cues.en: You could try to be like, “Oh, there’s a dog detecting neuron, and here’s a car detecting neuron.” And it turns out you can actually ask how those connect together.

cues.zh: 所以，你可以说，“哦，我有这个检测汽车的神经元。
cues.en: So, you can go say, “Oh, I have this car detecting neuron.

cues.zh: 它是怎么构建的？”而事实证明，在上一层中，它与窗户检测器、车轮检测器和车身检测器有着非常强的连接。
cues.en: How was it built?” And it turns out, in the previous layer, it’s connected really strongly to a window detector, and a wheel detector, and a car body detector.

cues.zh: 它会寻找汽车上方的窗户、下方的车轮，以及中间的汽车镀铬部分，几乎遍布各处，但尤其是在下半部分。
cues.en: And it looks for the window above the car, and the wheels below, and the car chrome in the middle, sort of everywhere, but especially on the lower part.

cues.zh: 这就是识别汽车的配方，对吧？
cues.en: And that’s sort of a recipe for a car, right?

cues.zh: 之前我们说过，机械可解释性想要的是找出算法，去问“运行的是什么算法？”而这里我们只是看神经网络的权重，读出了这个检测汽车的配方。
cues.en: Earlier, we said the thing we wanted from mech interp was to get algorithms to go and get, ask, “What is the algorithm that runs?” Well, here we’re just looking at the weights of the neural network and we’re reading off this recipe for detecting cars.

cues.zh: 这是个非常简单粗糙的配方，但它确实存在。
cues.en: It’s a very simple, crude recipe, but it’s there.

cues.zh: 我们把这个连接称为电路。
cues.en: And so we call that a circuit, this connection.

cues.zh: 好吧，问题在于并非所有神经元都是可解释的。
cues.en: Well, okay, so the problem is that not all of the neurons are interpretable.

cues.zh: 而且有理由认为——这个我们后面再深入——存在叠加假说，有理由认为有时候分析事物的正确单元是神经元的组合。
cues.en: And there’s reason to think, we can get into this more later, that there’s this superposition hypothesis, there’s reason to think that sometimes the right unit to analyze things is combinations of neurons.

cues.zh: 所以有时候并不是有一个单独的神经元代表比如汽车，而是实际上在你检测到汽车之后，模型会在下一层把汽车的一小部分藏在了一堆狗检测器里。
cues.en: So, sometimes it’s not that there’s a single neuron that represents, say, a car, but it actually turns out after you detect the car, the model hides a little bit of the car in the following layer, in a bunch of dog detectors.

cues.zh: 它为什么这么做？
cues.en: Why is it doing that?

cues.zh: 也许它只是不想在那个时候在汽车上花那么多功夫，就把它存起来，留着去……所以，结果就是，这种微妙的模式……有这么多神经元，你以为它们是狗检测器，也许它们主要就是干这个的，但它们都或多或少地参与在下一层中表示汽车。
cues.en: Well, maybe it just doesn’t want to do that much work on cars at that point, and it’s storing it away to go and… So, it turns out, then, that this sort of subtle pattern of… There’s all these neurons that you think are dog detectors, and maybe they’re primarily that, but they all a little bit contribute to representing a car in that next layer.

cues.zh: 好吗？
cues.en: Okay?

cues.zh: 所以，现在我们没法真的认为……可能仍然有某种东西，我不知道，你可以称之为汽车概念之类的，但它不再对应一个神经元了。
cues.en: So, now we can’t really think… There might still be something, I don’t know, you could call it a car concept or something, but it no longer corresponds to a neuron.

cues.zh: 所以，我们需要一个术语来称呼这类类似神经元的东西，这些我们原本希望神经元成为的东西，这些理想化的神经元。
cues.en: So, we need some term for these kind of neuron-like entities, these things that we would have liked the neurons to be, these idealized neurons.

cues.zh: 这些是好的神经元，但也许还有更多这样的东西以某种方式隐藏着。
cues.en: The things that are the nice neurons, but also maybe there’s more of them somehow hidden.

cues.zh: 我们把这些称为特征。
cues.en: And we call those features.

cues.zh: 那么什么是回路？
cues.en: And then what are circuits?

cues.zh: 回路就是特征之间的这些连接，对吧？
cues.en: So, circuits are these connections of features, right?

cues.zh: 当我们有一个汽车检测器，它连接到一个车窗检测器和一个车轮检测器，它寻找下方的车轮和上方的车窗，这就是一个回路。
cues.en: So, when we have the car detector and it’s connected to a window detector and a wheel detector, and it looks for the wheels below and the windows on top, that’s a circuit.

cues.zh: 回路就是由权重连接起来的特征集合，它们实现了算法。
cues.en: So, circuits are just collections of features connected by weights, and they implement algorithms.

cues.zh: 它们告诉我们特征是如何被使用的，如何被构建的，如何连接在一起的？
cues.en: So, they tell us how are features used, how are they built, how do they connect together?

cues.zh: 所以，也许值得试着明确一下这里的核心假设到底是什么？
cues.en: So, maybe it’s worth trying to pin down what really is the core hypothesis here?

cues.zh: 我认为核心假设就是我们所说的线性表示假设。
cues.en: And I think the core hypothesis is something we call the linear representation hypothesis.

cues.zh: 如果我们想想汽车检测器，它激活得越强，我们就越认为这意味着：“哦，模型越来越确信有一辆车存在。”或者如果它是代表汽车的某些神经元的组合，这个组合激活得越强，我们就越认为模型认为有一辆车存在。
cues.en: So, if we think about the car detector, the more it fires, the more we think of that as meaning, “Oh, the model is more and more confident that a car is present.” Or if it’s some combination of neurons that represent a car, the more that combination fires, the more we think the model thinks there’s a car present.

cues.zh: 不一定非得这样，对吧？
cues.en: This doesn’t have to be the case, right?

cues.zh: 你可以想象这样一种情况：有一个汽车检测神经元，你会想，“啊，如果它在1到2之间激活，那表示一种含义，但如果它在3到4之间激活，那含义就完全不同了。”那就会是一种非线性表示。
cues.en: You could imagine something where you have this car detector neuron and you think, “Ah, if it fires between one and two, that means one thing, but it means something totally different if it’s between three and four.” That would be a nonlinear representation.

cues.zh: 原则上，模型是可以做到这一点的。
cues.en: And in principle, models could do that.

cues.zh: 我觉得让模型这么做有点低效。
cues.en: I think it’s sort of inefficient for them to do.

cues.zh: 如果你试着想想要如何实现那样的计算，那其实是件挺麻烦的事。
cues.en: If you try to think about how you’d implement computation like that, it’s kind of an annoying thing to do.

cues.zh: 但原则上，模型是可以做到的。
cues.en: But in principle, models can do that.

cues.zh: 所以，把特征和电路这个框架理解为一种思考方式，其中一种思路就是我们把这些东西都当作线性的来看待。
cues.en: So, one way to think about the features and circuits sort of framework for thinking about things is that we’re thinking about things as being linear.

cues.zh: 我们的想法是，如果一个神经元或一组神经元激活得更多，那就意味着检测到了更多某种特定的东西。
cues.en: We’re thinking about that if a neuron or a combination of neurons fires more, that means more of a particular thing being detected.

cues.zh: 这就赋予了权重，一种非常清晰的解释，即这些实体之间的边，这些特征，然后那条边就有了意义。
cues.en: And then that gives weight, a very clean interpretation as these edges between these entities that these features, and that that edge then has a meaning.

cues.zh: 所以从某些方面来说，这就是核心的东西。
cues.en: So that’s, in some ways, the core thing.

cues.zh: 就像我们可以在神经元的语境之外讨论这个。
cues.en: It’s like we can talk about this outside the context of neurons.

cues.zh: 你熟悉 Word2Vec 的结果吗？
cues.en: Are you familiar with the Word2Vec results?

cues.zh: 嗯哼。
cues.en: Mm- hmm.

cues.zh: 你有 king – man + woman = queen。
cues.en: You have king – man + woman = queen.

cues.zh: 嗯，你能做那种算术的原因是因为你有一个线性表示。
cues.en: Well, the reason you can do that kind of arithmetic is because you have a linear representation.

cues.zh: 你能稍微解释一下那个表示吗？
cues.en: Can you actually explain that representation a little bit?

cues.zh: 首先，特征是一个激活方向。
cues.en: So first off, the feature is a direction of activation.

cues.zh: 是的，没错。
cues.en: Yeah, exactly.

cues.zh: 你可以那样做。
cues.en: You can do it that way.

cues.zh: 你能做那个——men + women，那个，Word2Vec 的东西吗？
cues.en: Can you do the – men + women, that, the Word2Vec stuff?

cues.zh: 你能解释一下那是什么吗，那个工作？
cues.en: Can you explain what that is, that work?

cues.zh: 好的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 所以，有一个非常——
cues.en: So, there’s this very-

cues.zh: 这是对我们所讨论内容的一个如此简单、清晰的解释。
cues.en: It’s such a simple, clean explanation of what we’re talking about.

cues.zh: 正是如此。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 有个非常著名的成果，Word2Vec，出自 Tomas Mikolov 等人，之后有大量后续工作对此展开探索。
cues.en: So, there’s this very famous result, Word2Vec, by Tomas Mikolov et al, and there’s been tons of follow-up work exploring this.

cues.zh: 有时我们会创建词嵌入，把每个词映射成一个向量。
cues.en: So, sometimes we create these word embeddings where we map every word to a vector.

cues.zh: 顺便说一句，如果你以前没想过这件事，这本身就挺疯狂的，对吧？
cues.en: I mean, that in itself, by the way, is kind of a crazy thing if you haven’t thought about it before, right?

cues.zh: 嗯哼。
cues.en: Mm-hmm.

cues.zh: 如果你刚在物理课上学了向量，然后我说“我要把字典里每个词都变成一个向量”，这想法挺疯狂的。
cues.en: If you just learned about vectors in physics class, and I’m like, “Oh, I’m going to actually turn every word in the dictionary into a vector,” that’s kind of a crazy idea.

cues.zh: 好。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 但你可以想象各种把词映射成向量的方式。
cues.en: But you could imagine all kinds of ways in which you might map words to vectors.

cues.zh: 但似乎当我们训练神经网络时，它们倾向于把词映射成向量，使得在特定意义上存在某种线性结构，也就是方向具有含义。
cues.en: But it seems like when we train neural networks, they like to go and map words to vectors such that there’s sort of linear structure in a particular sense, which is that directions have meaning.

cues.zh: 比如说，可能会有某个方向似乎大致对应性别，男性词汇会远离某个方向，女性词汇则在另一个方向。
cues.en: So, for instance, there will be some direction that seems to sort of correspond to gender, and male words will be far in one direction, and female words will be in another direction.

cues.zh: 而线性表示假说，你可以粗略地理解为，它实际上是在说这才是根本所在，一切不过是不同方向有不同含义，把不同的方向向量加在一起就能表示概念。
cues.en: And the linear representation hypothesis is, you could think of it roughly as saying that that’s actually the fundamental thing that’s going on, that everything is just different directions have meanings, and adding different direction vectors together can represent concepts.

cues.zh: Mikolov 的论文认真对待了这个想法，它的一个推论就是你可以玩这种对词做算术的游戏。
cues.en: And the Mikolov paper took that idea seriously, and one consequence of it is that you can do this game of playing arithmetic with words.

cues.zh: 所以，你可以拿 king，减去 man 这个词，再加上 woman 这个词。
cues.en: So, you can do king and you can subtract off the word man and add the word woman.

cues.zh: 于是你就像是在尝试切换性别。
cues.en: And so you’re sort of going and trying to switch the gender.

cues.zh: 确实，如果你这么做，结果会接近“女王”这个词。
cues.en: And indeed, if you do that, the result will sort of be close to the word queen.

cues.zh: 你还可以做其他事情，比如做寿司——日本+意大利，得到披萨，或者类似这样的不同组合，对吧？
cues.en: And you can do other things like you can do sushi – Japan + Italy and get pizza, or different things like this, right?

cues.zh: 所以从某种意义上说，这就是线性表示假说的核心。
cues.en: So this is, in some sense, the core of the linear representation hypothesis.

cues.zh: 你可以把它描述为关于向量空间的纯粹抽象概念。
cues.en: You can describe it just as a purely abstract thing about vector spaces.

cues.zh: 你可以把它描述为关于神经元激活的陈述，但它真正关乎的是方向具有意义这一属性。
cues.en: You can describe it as a statement about the activations of neurons, but it’s really about this property of directions having meaning.

cues.zh: 在某些方面，它甚至更微妙一些……我认为它主要关乎的是能够将事物相加这一属性，你可以独立地修改，比如性别和皇室属性，或者菜肴类型、国家，以及食物的概念，通过将它们相加来实现。
cues.en: And in some ways, it’s even a little subtler than… It’s really, I think, mostly about this property of being able to add things together, that you can independently modify, say gender and royalty, or cuisine type, or country, and the concept of food by adding them.

cues.zh: 你认为线性假设成立吗——
cues.en: Do you think the linear hypothesis holds-

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yes.

cues.zh: ……它带有尺度？
cues.en: … that carries scales?

cues.zh: 到目前为止，我觉得我看到的一切都与这个假设一致，而且它本来也不一定非得如此，对吧？
cues.en: So far, I think everything I have seen is consistent with this hypothesis, and it doesn’t have to be that way, right?

cues.zh: 你可以写出这样的神经网络：设定权重，使它们不具备线性表示，理解它们的正确方式并不是线性表示。
cues.en: You can write down neural networks where you write weights such that they don’t have linear representations, where the right way to understand them is not in terms of linear representations.

cues.zh: 但我认为我见过的每一个自然神经网络都具有这个性质。
cues.en: But I think every natural neural network I’ve seen has this property.

cues.zh: 最近有一篇论文，在某种程度上是在边缘上做了一些推进。
cues.en: There’s been one paper recently that there’s been some sort of pushing around the edge.

cues.zh: 所以，我认为最近有一些工作在研究多维特征，不是单一方向，而更像是一个方向流形。
cues.en: So, I think there’s been some work recently studying multidimensional features where rather than a single direction, it’s more like a manifold of directions.

cues.zh: 在我看来，这仍然像是一种线性表示。
cues.en: This, to me, still seems like a linear representation.

cues.zh: 然后还有一些其他论文提出，也许在非常小的模型里，你会得到非线性的表示。
cues.en: And then there’s been some other papers suggesting that maybe in very small models you get non-linear representations.

cues.zh: 我觉得这个问题还没有定论。
cues.en: I think that the jury’s still out on that.

cues.zh: 但我认为，到目前为止我们看到的一切都与线性表示假说一致，而这太不可思议了。
cues.en: But I think everything that we’ve seen so far has been consistent with the linear representation hypothesis, and that’s wild.

cues.zh: 它不一定非得是这样。
cues.en: It doesn’t have to be that way.

cues.zh: 然而我认为有大量证据表明，至少这一点是非常非常普遍的，而且到目前为止证据都与之一致。
cues.en: And yet I think that there’s a lot of evidence that certainly at least this is very, very widespread, and so far the evidence is consistent with that.

cues.zh: 我想你可能会说：“嗯，Christopher，这可真是压了很大的赌注。
cues.en: And I think one thing you might say is you might say, “Well, Christopher, that’s a lot to go and to ride on.

cues.zh: 如果我们不能确定这是真的，而你却把它当作真的来投入神经网络研究，这难道不危险吗？”
cues.en: If we don’t know for sure this is true, and you’re investing it in neural networks as though it is true, isn’t that dangerous?”

cues.zh: 但我觉得，认真对待假说并把它推到极限，其实是有价值的。
cues.en: But I think, actually, there’s a virtue in taking hypotheses seriously and pushing them as far as they can go.

cues.zh: 所以，也许有一天我们会发现某些与线性表示假设不符的东西，但科学中充满了曾经错误的假设和理论，我们通过把它们当作假设来工作，然后尽可能地把它们推到极限，从而学到了很多。
cues.en: So, it might be that someday we discover something that isn’t consistent with a linear representation hypothesis, but science is full of hypotheses and theories that were wrong, and we learned a lot by working under them as an assumption and then going and pushing them as far as we can.

cues.zh: 我想这就是库恩所说的常规科学的核心。
cues.en: I guess this is the heart of what Kuhn would call normal science.

cues.zh: 我不知道。
cues.en: I don’t know.

cues.zh: 如果你愿意，我们可以多聊聊——
cues.en: If you want, we can talk a lot about-

cues.zh: 库恩。
cues.en: Kuhn.

cues.zh: ……科学哲学以及——
cues.en: … philosophy of science and-

cues.zh: 这就引出了范式转移。
cues.en: That leads to the paradigm shift.

cues.zh: 所以是的，我喜欢这样，认真对待假设，并把它推向自然的结论。
cues.en: So yeah, I love it, taking the hypothesis seriously, and take it to a natural conclusion.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 缩放假设也是如此。
cues.en: Same with the scaling hypothesis.

cues.zh: 同样——
cues.en: Same-

cues.zh: 正是如此。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 正是如此。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 而且——
cues.en: And-

cues.zh: 我喜欢。
cues.en: I love it.

cues.zh: 我的一位同事，Tom Henighan，他以前是物理学家，给我做了一个非常好的类比，关于热质说，曾经我们以为热实际上是叫做热质的东西。
cues.en: One of my colleagues, Tom Henighan, who is a former physicist, made this really nice analogy to me of caloric theory where once upon a time, we thought that heat was actually this thing called caloric.

cues.zh: 热物体之所以会温暖冷物体，是因为热质在它们之间流动。
cues.en: And the reason hot objects would warm up cool objects is the caloric is flowing through them.

cues.zh: 因为我们太习惯用现代理论来思考热量，所以这听起来有点傻。
cues.en: And because we’re so used to thinking about heat in terms of the modern theory, that seems kind of silly.

cues.zh: 但实际上，很难设计出一个能推翻热质假说的实验。
cues.en: But it’s actually very hard to construct an experiment that disproves the caloric hypothesis.

cues.zh: 而且，相信热质说，你其实能做很多非常有用的工作。
cues.en: And you can actually do a lot of really useful work believing in caloric.

cues.zh: 比如，最初的燃烧引擎就是由相信热质理论的人开发出来的。
cues.en: For example, it turns out that the original combustion engines were developed by people who believed in the caloric theory.

cues.zh: 所以，我认为认真对待假说是有价值的，即使它们可能是错的。
cues.en: So, I think there’s a virtue in taking hypotheses seriously even when they might be wrong.

cues.zh: 是的，这里面有一个深刻的哲学真理。
cues.en: Yeah, there’s a deep philosophical truth to that.

cues.zh: 我对太空旅行，比如殖民火星，也有类似的感觉。
cues.en: That’s kind of how I feel about space travel, like colonizing Mars.

cues.zh: 有很多人批评这一点。
cues.en: There’s a lot of people that criticize that.

cues.zh: 我觉得，就算殖民火星这个假设不一定成立，只要我们认定必须殖民火星，为人类文明留个备份，也会催生一些有趣的工程突破，甚至科学突破。
cues.en: I think if you just assume we have to colonize Mars in order to have a backup for human civilization, even if that’s not true, that’s going to produce some interesting engineering and even scientific breakthroughs, I think.

cues.zh: 对。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 其实，我觉得还有一点也很有意思。
cues.en: Actually, this is another thing that I think is really interesting.

cues.zh: 所以，让一些人近乎非理性地执着于验证特定假设，对社会其实很有用，因为大多数科学假设最后都是错的，要维持科研士气、真正推进某件事，需要很大的投入。
cues.en: So, there’s a way in which I think it can be really useful for society to have people almost irrationally dedicated to investigating particular hypotheses because, well, it takes a lot to maintain scientific morale and really push on something when most scientific hypotheses end up being wrong.

cues.zh: 很多科学研究最后都没成，但这仍然很有用……有个关于 Geoff Hinton 的笑话，说他过去 50 年里每年都“发现了大脑的运作方式”。
cues.en: A lot of science doesn’t work out, and yet it’s very useful to… There’s a joke about Geoff Hinton, which is that Geoff Hinton has discovered how the brain works every year for the last 50 years.

cues.zh: 但我说这话是怀着深深的敬意，因为事实上，这反而促使他做出了一些非常出色的工作。
cues.en: But I say that with really deep respect because, in fact, actually, that led to him doing some really great work.

cues.zh: 是啊，他现在拿了诺贝尔奖。
cues.en: Yeah, he won the Nobel Prize now.

cues.zh: 现在谁在笑？
cues.en: Who’s laughing now?

cues.zh: 正是。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 正是。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 正是。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 我觉得人需要能够随时跳出来，认清自己该有的信心程度。
cues.en: I think one wants to be able to pop up and recognize the appropriate level of confidence.

cues.zh: 但我也觉得，直接这样想很有价值：“我基本上就假定，我就以这个问题可行、或者这大体是正确方向为前提。
cues.en: But I think there’s also a lot of value in just being like, “I’m going to essentially assume, I’m going to condition on this problem being possible or this being broadly the right approach.

cues.zh: 我就先这么假定一段时间，在这个框架里干活，拼命往前推。”如果社会上有许多人针对不同的事都这么做，那其实非常有用，能去——
cues.en: And I’m just going to go and assume that for a while and go and work within that, and push really hard on it.” And if society has lots of people doing that for different things, that’s actually really useful in terms of going and-

cues.zh: ……那其实非常有用，能去要么真正排除掉一些可能。
cues.en: … things that’s actually really useful in terms of going and either really ruling things out.

cues.zh: 我们可以说，“嗯，这没成功，但我们知道有人努力尝试过。”或者去追求那些确实能教会我们一些关于世界的东西。
cues.en: We can be like, “Well, that didn’t work and we know that somebody tried hard.” Or going and getting to something that does teach us something about the world.

cues.zh: 所以另一个有趣的假设是超级叠加假设。
cues.en: So another interesting hypothesis is the super superposition hypothesis.

cues.zh: 你能描述一下什么是叠加吗？
cues.en: Can you describe what superposition is?

cues.zh: 好的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 之前我们在讨论词缺陷，对吧？
cues.en: So earlier we were talking about word defect, right?

cues.zh: 我们谈到也许有一个方向对应性别，也许另一个对应皇室，另一个对应意大利，另一个对应食物，所有这些事情。
cues.en: And we were talking about how maybe you have one direction that corresponds to gender and maybe another that corresponds to royalty and another one that corresponds to Italy and another one that corresponds to food and all of these things.

cues.zh: 嗯，通常这些词嵌入可能有500维、1000维。
cues.en: Well, oftentimes maybe these word embeddings, they might be 500 dimensions, a thousand dimensions.

cues.zh: 所以如果你相信所有这些方向都是正交的，那么你只能有500个概念。
cues.en: And so if you believe that all of those directions were orthogonal, then you could only have 500 concepts.

cues.zh: 而且我爱披萨。
cues.en: And I love pizza.

cues.zh: 但如果我要列出英语里最重要的500个概念，意大利大概不会……至少意大利显然不一定会是其中之一，对吧？
