cues.en: But if I was going to go and give the 500 most important concepts in the English language, probably Italy wouldn’t be… it’s not obvious, at least that Italy would be one of them, right?

cues.zh: 因为你得先有单数和复数、动词和名词、形容词这些东西。
cues.en: Because you have to have things like plural and singular and verb and noun and adjective.

cues.zh: 在讲到意大利和日本之前，我们还有很多东西要讲，而且世界上有很多国家。
cues.en: And there’s a lot of things we have to get to before we get to Italy and Japan, and there’s a lot of countries in the world.

cues.zh: 那么，模型怎么可能同时满足线性表示假说为真，又能表示比它拥有的方向更多的东西呢？
cues.en: And so how might it be that models could simultaneously have the linear representation hypothesis be true and also represent more things than they have directions?

cues.zh: 那这意味着什么呢？
cues.en: So what does that mean?

cues.zh: 好吧，如果线性表示假说为真，那一定发生了某种有趣的事情。
cues.en: Well, okay, so if linear representation hypothesis is true, something interesting has to be going on.

cues.zh: 在我们结束前，我再告诉你一件有趣的事，那就是之前我们谈到的所有这些多语义神经元，这些在观察Inception V1时发现的神经元，比如汽车检测器和曲线检测器等，它们对许多非常连贯的事物作出反应。
cues.en: Now, I’ll tell you one more interesting thing before we go, and we do that, which is earlier we were talking about all these polysemantic neurons, these neurons that when we were looking at inception V1, these nice neurons that the car detector and the curve detector and so on that respond to lots of very coherent things.

cues.zh: 但也有很多神经元对一系列不相关的事物作出反应。
cues.en: But it’s lots of neurons that respond to a bunch of unrelated things.

cues.zh: 这也是一个有趣的现象。
cues.en: And that’s also an interesting phenomenon.

cues.zh: 而且事实证明，即使是这些非常非常干净的神经元，如果你观察微弱的激活，也就是当它激活到最大激活值的5%时，那真的不是它期望的核心事物。
cues.en: And it turns out as well that even these neurons that are really, really clean, if you look at the weak activations, so if you look at the activations where it’s activating 5% of the maximum activation, it’s really not the core thing that it’s expecting.

cues.zh: 例如，如果你观察一个曲线检测器，看看它5%活跃的地方，你可以把它解释为噪音，或者它在那里可能在做别的事情。
cues.en: So if you look at a curve detector for instance, and you look at the places where it’s 5% active, you could interpret it just as noise or it could be that it’s doing something else there.

cues.zh: 可以吗？
cues.en: Okay?

cues.zh: 那怎么会这样呢？
cues.en: So how could that be?

cues.zh: 嗯，数学里有个很神奇的东西叫压缩感知，它其实是个非常令人惊讶的事实：如果你有一个高维空间，把它投影到低维空间，通常你没法反投影回去拿回你的高维向量，因为信息被丢掉了。
cues.en: Well, there’s this amazing thing in mathematics called compressed sensing, and it’s actually this very surprising fact where if you have a high dimensional space and you project it into a low dimensional space, ordinarily you can’t go and sort of un-projected and get back your high dimensional vector, you threw information away.

cues.zh: 这就像你没法求一个矩形矩阵的逆。
cues.en: This is like you can’t invert a rectangular matrix.

cues.zh: 你只能求方阵的逆。
cues.en: You can only invert square matrices.

cues.zh: 但事实证明，这其实并不完全对。
cues.en: But it turns out that that’s actually not quite true.

cues.zh: 如果我告诉你那个高维向量是稀疏的，也就是大部分是零，那么事实证明你往往能以极高的概率把高维向量找回来。
cues.en: If I tell you that the high-dimensional vector was sparse, so it’s mostly zeros, then it turns out that you can often go and find back the high-dimensional vector with very high probability.

cues.zh: 所以这是个令人惊讶的事实，对吧？
cues.en: So that’s a surprising fact, right?

cues.zh: 你可以拥有这个高维向量空间，只要事物是稀疏的，就能把它投影下来，得到低维投影，这样就行。
cues.en: It says that you can have this high-dimensional vector space, and as long as things are sparse, you can project it down, you can have a lower-dimensional projection of it, and that works.

cues.zh: 所以迷信假说说的是，比如神经网络里就是这样，词嵌入里也是这样。
cues.en: So the superstition hypothesis is saying that that’s what’s going on in neural networks, for instance, that’s what’s going on in word embeddings.

cues.zh: 词嵌入能够同时让方向成为有意义的东西，利用它们在一个相当高维空间上运作这一点，实际上……而且这些概念是稀疏的，你通常不会同时谈论日本和意大利。
cues.en: The word embeddings are able to simultaneously have directions be the meaningful thing, and by exploiting the fact that they’re operating on a fairly high-dimensional space, they’re actually… and the fact that these concepts are sparse, you usually aren’t talking about Japan and Italy at the same time.

cues.zh: 大多数概念、大多数情况下，日本和意大利都是零。
cues.en: Most of those concepts, in most instances, Japan and Italy are both zero.

cues.zh: 它们根本不存在。
cues.en: They’re not present at all.

cues.zh: 如果真是这样，那么你就可以有远多于维度的、有意义的这类方向，这些特征。
cues.en: And if that’s true, then you can go and have it be the case that you can have many more of these sort of directions that are meaningful, these features than you have dimensions.

cues.zh: 同样地，当我们谈论神经元时，你可以拥有比神经元更多的概念。
cues.en: And similarly, when we’re talking about neurons, you can have many more concepts than you have neurons.

cues.zh: 所以这就是高层次的超级假设。
cues.en: So that’s at a high level, the superstition hypothesis.

cues.zh: 现在它有一个更疯狂的推论，那就是神经网络可能不仅仅是表示方式像这样，计算方式也可能像这样。
cues.en: Now it has this even wilder implication, which is to go and say that neural networks, it may not just be the case that the representations are like this, but the computation may also be like this.

cues.zh: 它们之间的所有连接。
cues.en: The connections between all of them.

cues.zh: 所以从某种意义上说，神经网络可能是更大、更稀疏的神经网络的影子。
cues.en: And so in some sense, neural networks may be shadows of much larger sparser neural networks.

cues.zh: 而我们看到的只是这些投影。
cues.en: And what we see are these projections.

cues.zh: 而迷信假说最强的版本，就是要认真对待它，并说在某种意义上确实存在这样一个 upstairs 模型，其中神经元非常稀疏且全是 interpleural 的，它们之间的权重是这些非常稀疏的回路。
cues.en: And the strongest version of superstition hypothesis would be to take that really seriously and sort of say there actually is in some sense this upstairs model where the neurons are really sparse and all interpleural, and the weights between them are these really sparse circuits.

cues.zh: 而这正是我们在研究的东西。
cues.en: And that’s what we’re studying.

cues.zh: 我们观察到的是证据的影子。
cues.en: And the thing that we’re observing is the shadow of evidence.

cues.zh: 我们需要找到原始对象。
cues.en: We need to find the original object.

cues.zh: 而学习的过程，就是试图构造对 upstairs 模型的一种压缩，且在投影过程中不丢失太多信息。
cues.en: And the process of learning is trying to construct a compression of the upstairs model that doesn’t lose too much information in the projection.

cues.zh: 是啊，就是找到如何高效地拟合它之类的。
cues.en: Yeah, it’s finding how to fit it efficiently or something like this.

cues.zh: 梯度下降正在做这件事，事实上这也就是说，梯度下降可以只是表示一个稠密神经网络，但它也说明梯度下降在隐式地搜索那些极其稀疏的模型空间，这些模型可以投影到这个低维空间。
cues.en: The gradient descent is doing this and in fact, so this sort of says that gradient descent, it could just represent a dense neural network, but it sort of says that gradient descent is implicitly searching over the space of extremely sparse models that could be projected into this low-dimensional space.

cues.zh: 有很多人投身于稀疏神经网络的研究，你可以设计边稀疏、激活也稀疏的神经网络。
cues.en: And this large body of work of people going and trying to study sparse neural networks where you go and you have… you could design neural networks where the edges are sparse and the activations are sparse.

cues.zh: 我的感觉是，这类工作虽然看上去很有原则、很有道理，但整体来看，成效并没有那么好。
cues.en: And my sense is that work has generally, it feels very principled, it makes so much sense, and yet that work hasn’t really panned out that well, is my impression broadly.

cues.zh: 我觉得一个可能的解释是，神经网络其实在某种意义上已经是稀疏的了。
cues.en: And I think that a potential answer for that is that actually the neural network is already sparse in some sense.

cues.zh: 你本来是想去做这件事。
cues.en: You were trying to go and do this.

cues.zh: 梯度下降其实在背后替你更高效地搜索了稀疏模型的空间，并学到了最有效的那个稀疏模型。
cues.en: Gradient descent was actually behind the scenes going and searching more efficiently than you could through the space of sparse models and going and learning whatever sparse model was most efficient.

cues.zh: 然后要想办法把它优雅地折叠起来，以便方便地在 GPU 上运行，因为 GPU 擅长做密集矩阵乘法。
cues.en: And then figuring out how to fold it down nicely to go and run conveniently on your GPU, which does as nice dense matrix multiplies.

cues.zh: 这一点你没法超越。
cues.en: And that you just can’t beat that.

cues.zh: 你觉得一个神经网络里能塞进多少个概念？
cues.en: How many concepts do you think can be shoved into a neural network?

cues.zh: 取决于它们有多稀疏。
cues.en: Depends on how sparse they are.

cues.zh: 所以可能存在一个由参数数量决定的上限，因为你仍然需要有连接的权重把它们连起来。
cues.en: So there’s probably an upper bound from the number of parameters because you still have to have print weights that go and connect them together.

cues.zh: 这就是一个上限。
cues.en: So that’s one upper bound.

cues.zh: 事实上，压缩感知和 Johnson-Lindenstrauss 引理等领域有这些漂亮的结果，它们基本上告诉你，如果你有一个向量空间，想要得到几乎正交的向量——这大概正是你这里想要的。
cues.en: There are in fact all these lovely results from compressed sensing and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma and things like this that they basically tell you that if you have a vector space and you want to have almost orthogonal vectors, which is sort of probably the thing that you want here.

cues.zh: 所以你会说：“好吧，我打算放弃让我的概念、我的特征严格正交，但我希望它们不要互相干扰太多。
cues.en: So you’re going to say, “Well, I’m going to give up on having my concepts, my features be strictly orthogonal, but I’d like them to not interfere that much.

cues.zh: 我得要求它们几乎正交。”
cues.en: I’m going to have to ask them to be almost orthogonal.”

cues.zh: 那么这就说明，一旦你设定了一个阈值，规定你能接受多大的余弦相似度，这实际上在你拥有的神经元数量上是指数级的。
cues.en: Then this would say that it’s actually for, once you set a threshold for what you’re willing to accept in terms of how much cosine similarity there is, that’s actually exponential in the number of neurons that you have.

cues.zh: 所以在某个点上，这甚至都不会成为限制因素，但那里有一些漂亮的结果。
cues.en: So at some point, that’s not going to even be the limiting factor, but there’s some beautiful results there.

cues.zh: 而事实上，从某种意义上说，情况可能比这还要好，因为那只是说任何随机的特征集合都可能被激活。
cues.en: And in fact, it’s probably even better than that in some sense because that’s sort of for saying that any random set of features could be active.

cues.zh: 但事实上，特征具有某种相关性结构，有些特征更可能共同出现，而另一些则不太可能共同出现。
cues.en: But in fact the features have sort of a correlational structure where some features are more likely to co-occur and other ones are less likely to co-occur.

cues.zh: 所以，神经网络，我的嘉宾会认为，在打包东西方面可以做得很好，以至于这可能不是限制因素。
cues.en: And so neural networks, my guest would be, could do very well in terms of going and packing things to the point that’s probably not the limiting factor.

cues.zh: 多义性这个问题是如何进入画面的？
cues.en: How does the problem of polysemanticity enter the picture here?

cues.zh: 多义性是我们观察到的一种现象，你观察许多神经元，神经元并不只是代表一个概念，它不是一个干净的特征。
cues.en: Polysemanticity is this phenomenon we observe where you look at many neurons and the neuron doesn’t just sort of represent one concept, it’s not a clean feature.

cues.zh: 它对一堆不相关的事物都有响应。
cues.en: It responds to a bunch of unrelated things.

cues.zh: 而叠加可以看作是一个假设，用来解释多义性的观察结果。
cues.en: And superstition you can think of as being a hypothesis that explains the observation of polysemanticity.

cues.zh: 所以多义性是观察到的现象，叠加是一个假设，可以解释它以及其他一些事情。
cues.en: So polysemanticity is this observed phenomenon and superstition is a hypothesis that would explain it along with some other things.

cues.zh: 所以这让机制可解释性变得更加困难。
cues.en: So that makes Mechinterp more difficult.

cues.zh: 对。
cues.en: Right.

cues.zh: 所以如果你想从单个神经元的角度去理解，而你又有多义神经元，那你就麻烦大了。
cues.en: So if you’re trying to understand things in terms of individual neurons and you have polysemantic neurons, you’re in an awful lot of trouble.

cues.zh: 最简单的回答就是：“好吧，你在看神经元，你想理解它们。
cues.en: The easiest answer is like, “Okay, well you’re looking at the neurons, you’re trying to understand them.

cues.zh: 这个神经元对很多东西都有响应。
cues.en: This one responds for a lot of things.

cues.zh: 它没有一个清晰的含义。
cues.en: It doesn’t have a nice meaning.

cues.zh: 好吧，这很糟糕。”你还可以问的另一个问题是，最终我们想理解的是权重。
cues.en: Okay, that’s bad.” Another thing you could ask is ultimately we want to understand the weights.

cues.zh: 如果你有两个多义神经元，每个对三样东西有响应，另一个神经元也对三样东西有响应，它们之间还有一个权重，那意味着什么？
cues.en: And if you have two polysemantic neurons and each one responds to three things and then the other neuron responds to three things and you have a wait between them, what does that mean?

cues.zh: 是不是意味着这三样东西之间，存在这九种交互？
cues.en: Does it mean that all three, there’s these nine interactions going on?

cues.zh: 这非常奇怪，但背后还有一个更深层的原因，这与神经网络在非常高维的空间中运作有关。
cues.en: It’s a very weird thing, but there’s also a deeper reason, which is related to the fact that neural networks operate on really high dimensional spaces.

cues.zh: 所以我说过，我们的目标是理解神经网络，理解它的机制。
cues.en: So I said that our goal was to understand neural networks and understand the mechanisms.

cues.zh: 你可能会说：“嗯，它不过就是个数学函数。
cues.en: And one thing you might say is, “Well, it’s just a mathematical function.

cues.zh: 为什么不直接看它呢，对吧？”我最早做的项目之一，研究的是把二维空间映射到二维空间的神经网络，你可以用一种很漂亮的方式来解读它，就像弯曲流形。
cues.en: Why not just look at it, right?” One of the earliest projects I did studied these neural networks that mapped two-dimensional spaces to two-dimensional spaces, and you can sort of interpret them in this beautiful way is like bending manifolds.

cues.zh: 为什么我们不能这么做呢？
cues.en: Why can’t we do that?

cues.zh: 因为当空间维度更高时，这个空间的体积在某种意义上是你输入数量的指数级。
cues.en: Well, as you have a higher dimensional space, the volume of that space in some sense is exponential in the number of inputs you have.

cues.zh: 所以你不能直接去可视化它。
cues.en: And so you can’t just go and visualize it.

cues.zh: 所以我们得想办法把它拆开。
cues.en: So we somehow need to break that apart.

cues.zh: 我们需要想办法把这个指数级的空间拆成一堆东西，拆成非指数级数量的东西，让我们可以独立地去推理。
cues.en: We need to somehow break that exponential space into a bunch of things, some non-exponential number of things that we can reason about independently.

cues.zh: 而独立性至关重要，因为正是这种独立性让你不必去考虑所有指数级的组合情况。
cues.en: And the independence is crucial because it’s the independence that allows you to not have to think about all the exponential combinations of things.

cues.zh: 而事物是单义的，事物只有一个含义，事物有含义，这正是让你能够独立地思考它们的关键。
cues.en: And things being monosomatic, things only having one meaning, things having a meaning, that is the key thing that allows you to think about them independently.

cues.zh: 所以我认为，如果你想问我们为什么要追求可解释的单义特征，最深层的原因，我认为这才是真正深层的原因。
cues.en: And so I think if you want the deepest reason why we want to have interpretable monosomatic features, I think that’s really the deep reason.

cues.zh: 所以这里的目标，正如你最近的工作一直所追求的那样，就是我们如何从一个具有多义特征、一团乱麻的神经网络中提取出单义特征。
cues.en: And so the goal here as your recent work has been aiming at is how do we extract the monosomatic features from a neural net that has polysemantic features and all this mess.

cues.zh: 是的，我们观察到这些多义神经元，我们假设正在发生的就是叠加。
cues.en: Yes, we observe these polysemantic neurons, we hypothesize that’s what’s going on is superposition.

cues.zh: 如果存在叠加现象，其实有一种成熟的技术，算是比较有原则的做法，那就是字典学习。
cues.en: And if superposition is what’s going on, there’s actually a sort of well-established technique that is sort of the principled thing to do, which is dictionary learning.

cues.zh: 结果发现，如果你做字典学习，特别是用一种高效的方式，在某种意义上也能很好地正则化，叫做稀疏自编码器。
cues.en: And it turns out if you do dictionary learning in particular, if you do sort of a nice efficient way that in some sense sort of nicely regularizes that as well called a sparse auto encoder.

cues.zh: 如果你训练一个稀疏自编码器，这些漂亮的可解释特征就会开始自动浮现出来，而之前根本没有。
cues.en: If you train a sparse auto encoder, these beautiful interpretable features start to just fall out where there weren’t any beforehand.

cues.zh: 所以这不是你一定能预测到的，但结果发现它效果非常非常好。
cues.en: So that’s not a thing that you would necessarily predict, but it turns out that works very, very well.

cues.zh: 对我来说，这似乎是对线性表示和叠加的一种相当重要的验证。
cues.en: To me, that seems like some non-trivial validation of linear representations and superposition.

cues.zh: 所以用字典学习，你并不是在寻找特定类型的类别。
cues.en: So with dictionary learning, you’re not looking for particular kind of categories.

cues.zh: 你不知道它们是什么，它们就是自己涌现出来的。
cues.en: You don’t know what they are, they just emerge.

cues.zh: 正是如此。
cues.en: Exactly.

cues.zh: 这就回到了我们之前说的：我们不做任何假设。
cues.en: And this gets back to our earlier point when we’re not making assumptions.

cues.zh: 梯度下降比我们更聪明，所以我们不对那里存在什么做假设。
cues.en: Gradient descent is smarter than us, so we’re not making assumptions about what’s there.

cues.zh: 我是说，当然可以那么做，对吧？
cues.en: I mean, one certainly could do that, right?

cues.zh: 你可以假设存在某个 PHP 特性，然后去搜索它，但我们不这么做。
cues.en: One could assume that there’s a PHP feature and go and search for it, but we’re not doing that.

cues.zh: 我们的意思是，我们不知道那里会有什么。
cues.en: We’re saying we don’t know what’s going to be there.

cues.zh: 相反，我们只是让稀疏自编码器去发现那里存在的东西。
cues.en: Instead, we’re just going to go and let the sparse auto encoder discover the things that are there.

cues.zh: 那你能谈谈去年十月那篇关于单义性的论文吗？
cues.en: So can you talk toward monosematicity paper from October last year?

cues.zh: 我听说有很多不错的突破性成果。
cues.en: I heard a lot of nice breakthrough results.

cues.zh: 你这么说真是太客气了。
cues.en: That’s very kind of you to describe it that way.

cues.zh: 是的，我是说，这是我们第一次真正成功使用稀疏自编码器。
cues.en: Yeah, I mean, this was our first real success using sparse autoencoders.

cues.zh: 我们拿了一个单层模型，结果发现，如果你对它做字典学习，就会发现所有这些非常好的可解释特征。
cues.en: So we took a one-layer model, and it turns out if you go and you do dictionary learning on it, you find all these really nice interpretable features.

cues.zh: 所以阿拉伯语特征、希伯来语特征、Base64 特征，都是我们深入研究过的例子，并且确实证明了它们就是我们以为的那样。
cues.en: So the Arabic feature, the Hebrew feature, the Base64 features were some examples that we studied in a lot of depth and really showed that they were what we thought they were.

cues.zh: 事实证明，如果你把一个模型训练得更好一倍，再训练两个不同的模型并做字典学习，你会在两者中找到类似的特征。
cues.en: Turns out if you train a model twice as well and train two different models and do dictionary learning, you find analogous features in both of them.

cues.zh: 所以这很有趣。
cues.en: So that’s fun.

cues.zh: 你会发现各种各样的不同特征。
cues.en: You find all kinds of different features.

cues.zh: 所以那其实只是在证明这方法是可行的。
cues.en: So that was really just showing that this works.

cues.zh: 我应该提一下，Cunningham 等人差不多在同一时间也得到了非常相似的结果。
cues.en: And I should mention that there was this Cunningham and all that had very similar results around the same time.

cues.zh: 做这类小规模实验并发现它确实有效，这挺有意思的。
cues.en: There’s something fun about doing these kinds of small scale experiments and finding that it’s actually working.

cues.zh: 是啊，而且这里的结构非常丰富。
cues.en: Yeah, well, and that there’s so much structure here.

cues.zh: 所以也许退一步说，有一段时间我以为所有这些机制性插值工作，最终结果会是我能解释为什么它非常困难且难以处理。
cues.en: So maybe stepping back, for a while I thought that maybe all this mechanistic interpolate work, the end result was going to be that I would have an explanation for why it was sort of very hard and not going to be tractable.

cues.zh: 我们会说，“好吧，存在这个超替换问题，结果超替换真的很难，我们有点完蛋了，但事实并非如此。
cues.en: We’d be like, “Well, there’s this problem with supersession and it turns out supersession is really hard and we’re kind of screwed, but that’s not what happened.

cues.zh: 事实上，一个非常自然简单的技术就奏效了。
cues.en: In fact, a very natural simple technique just works.

cues.zh: 所以这其实是一个非常好的情况。
cues.en: And so then that’s actually a very good situation.

cues.zh: 我认为这是一个相当难的研究问题，有很多研究风险，它很可能仍然会失败，但我认为当它开始奏效时，一些非常显著的研究风险已经被我们抛在身后了。
cues.en: I think this is a sort of hard research problem and it’s got a lot of research risk and it might still very well fail, but I think that some very significant amount of research risk was put behind us when that started to work.

cues.zh: 你能描述一下，用这种方式可以提取出哪些类型的特征吗？
cues.en: Can you describe what kind of features can be extracted in this way?

cues.zh: 嗯，这取决于你正在研究的模型。
cues.en: Well, so it depends on the model that you’re studying.

cues.zh: 模型越大，这些特征就会越复杂。
cues.en: So the larger the model, the more sophisticated they’re going to be.

cues.zh: 我们可能过一会儿会谈谈后续工作。
cues.en: And we’ll probably talk about follow up work in a minute.

cues.zh: 但在这些单层模型里，我认为非常常见的东西是语言，既包括编程语言也包括自然语言。
cues.en: But in these one layer models, so some very common things I think were languages, both programming languages and natural languages.

cues.zh: 有很多特征是针对特定语境中的特定单词的，所以……
cues.en: There were a lot of features that were specific words in specific contexts, so the.

cues.zh: 我觉得真正理解这件事的方式是，这个特征大概是说“后面很可能跟一个名词”。
cues.en: And I think really the way to think about this is that the is likely about to be followed by a noun.

cues.zh: 所以你可以把它看作这个特征，但也可以把它看作是在预测某个特定名词的特征。
cues.en: So you could think of this as the feature, but you could also think of this as protecting a specific noun feature.

cues.zh: 还会有一些特征会在比如法律文档、数学文档之类的语境中针对“the”触发。
cues.en: And there would be these features that would fire for the in the context of say, a legal document or a mathematical document or something like this.

cues.zh: 所以在数学语境下，你会说预测向量或矩阵这类数学词汇，而在其他语境下你会预测别的东西，这很常见。
cues.en: And so maybe in the context of math, you’re like the, and then predict vector or matrix, all these mathematical words, whereas in other contexts you would predict other things, that was common.

cues.zh: 基本上我们需要聪明的人来给看到的东西打标签。
cues.en: And basically we need clever humans to assign labels to what we’re seeing.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yes.

cues.zh: 所以它做的唯一一件事就是帮你把东西展开。
cues.en: So the only thing this is doing is that sort of unfolding things for you.

cues.zh: 所以如果所有东西都折叠在上面，序列化把所有东西都叠在自己身上，你根本看不清，这就是在把它展开。
cues.en: So if everything was sort of folded over top of it, serialization folded everything on top of itself and you can’t really see it, this is unfolding it.

cues.zh: 但现在你仍然有一个非常复杂的东西要去理解。
cues.en: But now you still have a very complex thing to try to understand.

cues.zh: 于是你得花一番功夫去理解这些是什么，有些还非常微妙。
cues.en: So then you have to do a bunch of work understanding what these are, and some are really subtle.

cues.zh: 即便在这个单层模型里，关于 Unicode 也有一些很酷的东西，当然有些语言是用 Unicode 的，而分词器不一定为每个 Unicode 字符都准备专门的 token。
cues.en: There’s some really cool things even in this one layer model about Unicode, where of course some languages are in Unicode, and the tokenizer won’t necessarily have a dedicated token for every Unicode character.

cues.zh: 所以相反，你会得到这些交替 token 的模式，每个 token 代表一个 Unicode 字符的一半。
cues.en: So instead, what you’ll have is you’ll have these patterns of alternating token or alternating tokens that each represent half of a Unicode character.

cues.zh: 还有一个不同的特征会在对立的那些上激活，就像：“好了，我刚完成一个字符，去预测下一个前缀。”
cues.en: And you have a different feature that goes and activates on the opposing ones to be like, “Okay, I just finished a character, go and predict next prefix.

cues.zh: 然后好，我在前缀上，预测一个合理的后缀。你得来回交替。
cues.en: Then okay, I’m on the prefix, predict a reasonable suffix.” And you have to alternate back and forth.

cues.zh: 所以这些交换层模型真的很有意思。
cues.en: So these swap layer models are really interesting.

cues.zh: 我的意思是，还有一点你可能会想：“好吧，应该只有一个 Base64 特征吧”，但事实证明其实有一堆 Base64 特征，因为你可以把英文文本编码成 Base64，而它的 Base64 token 分布和普通情况非常不同。
cues.en: And I mean there’s another thing that you might think, “Okay, there would just be one Base64 feature, but it turns out there’s actually a bunch of Base64 features because you can have English text encoded as Base64, and that has a very different distribution of Base64 tokens than regular.

cues.zh: 分词方面也有一些可以利用的东西。
cues.en: And there’s some things about tokenization as well that it can exploit.

cues.zh: 还有各种好玩的东西。
cues.en: And I don’t know, there’s all kinds of fun stuff.

cues.zh: 给正在发生的事情打标签，这个任务有多难？
cues.en: How difficult is the task of assigning labels to what’s going on?

cues.zh: 这能由 AI 自动化吗？
cues.en: Can this be automated by AI?

cues.zh: 嗯，我觉得这取决于特征，也取决于你有多信任你的 AI。
cues.en: Well, I think it depends on the feature, and it also depends on how much you trust your AI.

cues.zh: 所以有很多工作在搞自动化互操作。
cues.en: So there’s a lot of work doing automated interoperability.

cues.zh: 我觉得那是个非常令人兴奋的方向，我们做了相当多的自动化互操作，让 Claude 去给我们的特征打标签。
cues.en: I think that’s a really exciting direction, and we do a fair amount of automated interoperability and have Claude go and label our features.

cues.zh: 有没有一些有趣的时刻，它完全对或者完全错？
cues.en: Is there some fun moments where it’s totally right or it’s totally wrong?

cues.zh: 有，我觉得很常见的是它说一些很笼统的话，某种意义上是对的，但并没有真正抓住正在发生的事情的具体细节。
cues.en: Yeah, well, I think it’s very common that it says something very general, which is true in some sense, but not really picking up on the specific of what’s going on.

cues.zh: 我觉得这情况挺常见的。
cues.en: So I think that’s a pretty common situation.

cues.zh: 你不知道我有个特别逗的。
cues.en: You don’t know that I have a particularly amusing one.

cues.zh: 有意思。
cues.en: That’s interesting.

cues.zh: 那个小缺口在于它是对的，但没能触及事物深层的细微之处。
cues.en: That little gap between it is true, but it doesn’t quite get to the deep nuance of a thing.

cues.zh: 这是个普遍的挑战，能说出一个真实的点已经很了不起了，但有时就是缺少深度。
cues.en: That’s a general challenge, it’s already an incredible caution that can say a true thing, but it’s missing the depth sometimes.

cues.zh: 在这个语境下，就像ARC挑战那种智商测试。
cues.en: And in this context, it’s like the ARC challenge, the sort of IQ type of tests.

cues.zh: 感觉搞清楚一个特征代表什么，就像要解开一个小谜题。
cues.en: It feels like figuring out what a feature represents is a little puzzle you have to solve.

cues.zh: 对。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我觉得有时候它们简单些，有时候也难些。
cues.en: And I think that sometimes they’re easier and sometimes they’re harder as well.

cues.zh: 是啊，我觉得这挺棘手的。
cues.en: Yeah, I think that’s tricky.

cues.zh: 还有一点我不太确定，也许某种程度上这是我的审美偏好在起作用，但我试着给你一个合理的解释。
cues.en: There’s another thing which I don’t know, maybe in some ways this is my aesthetic coming in, but I’ll try to give you a rationalization.

cues.zh: 其实我对自动化互操作性有点怀疑，部分原因是我希望人类能理解神经网络。
cues.en: I’m actually a little suspicious of automated interoperability, and I think that partly just that I want humans to understand neural networks.

cues.zh: 如果神经网络替我理解了，我不太喜欢这样，但我确实有点……在某些方面，我有点像那些数学家，他们会说：“如果是计算机自动化的证明，那不算数。”他们不会理解的。
cues.en: And if the neural network is understanding it for me, I don’t quite like that, but I do have a bit of… In some ways, I’m sort of like the mathematicians who are like, “If there’s a computer automated proof, it doesn’t count.” They won’t understand it.

cues.zh: 但我也确实认为存在这种关于信任的信任的反思型问题，有一个著名的演讲讲到，当你写计算机程序时，你必须信任你的编译器。
cues.en: But I do also think that there is this kind of reflections on trusting trust type issue where there’s this famous talk about when you’re writing a computer program, you have to trust your compiler.

cues.zh: 如果你的编译器里有恶意软件，那它就可以把恶意软件注入到下一个编译器里，你就会陷入麻烦，对吧？
cues.en: And if there was malware in your compiler, then it could go and inject malware into the next compiler and you’d be kind of in trouble, right?

cues.zh: 如果你用神经网络去验证神经网络是否安全，你所依赖的假设就是：“好吧，这个神经网络可能不安全，你得担心它会不会以某种方式坑你。”
cues.en: Well, if you’re using neural networks to go and verify that your neural networks are safe, the hypothesis that you’re trusting for is like, “Okay, well the neural network maybe isn’t safe and you have to worry about is there some way that it could be screwing with you?

cues.zh: 我觉得目前这还不是大问题，但长远来看我确实在想，如果我们必须用非常强大的AI系统去审计我们的AI系统，那真的可信吗？
cues.en: I think that’s not a big concern now, but I do wonder in the long run, if we have to use really powerful AI systems to go and audit our AI systems, is that actually something we can trust?

cues.zh: 但也许我只是在自我合理化，因为我就是希望我们能走到人类理解一切的那一步。
cues.en: But maybe I’m just rationalizing because I just want us to have to get to a point where humans understand everything.

cues.zh: 是啊，这挺搞笑的，尤其是我们在讨论AI安全、寻找与AI安全相关的特征时，比如欺骗之类的。
cues.en: Yeah, I mean that’s hilarious, especially as we talk about AI safety and looking for features that would be relevant to AI safety, like deception and so on.

cues.zh: 那我们来聊聊2024年5月的《Scaling Monosematicity》论文。
cues.en: So let’s talk about the Scaling Monosematicity paper in May 2024.

cues.zh: 好的。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 那么，要扩展到Claude 3 Sonnet上应用，需要付出什么？
cues.en: So what did it take to scale this, to apply to Claude 3 Sonnet?

cues.zh: 嗯，大量GPU。
cues.en: Well, a lot of GPUs.

cues.zh: 多得多的GPU。
cues.en: A lot more GPUs.

cues.zh: 明白了。
cues.en: Got it.

cues.zh: 但我的一位队友Tom Henighan参与了最初的缩放定律研究，他从很早开始就感兴趣的一个问题是：互操作性是否存在缩放定律？
cues.en: But one of my teammates, Tom Henighan was involved in the original scaling laws work, and something that he was sort of interested in from very early on is are there scaling laws for interoperability?

cues.zh: 所以这项工作开始取得成功、我们开始让稀疏自编码器跑通时，他立刻很感兴趣的是：把稀疏自编码器做大的缩放定律是什么，以及这和把基础模型做大有什么关系？
cues.en: And so something he immediately did when this work started to succeed, and we started to have sparse autoencoders work, was he became very interested in what are the scaling laws for making sparse autoencoders larger and how does that relate to making the base model larger?

cues.zh: 结果发现这效果非常好，你可以用它来推算，比如训练一个给定大小的稀疏自编码器，应该用多少token来训练等等。
cues.en: And so it turns out this works really well and you can use it to sort of project, if you train a sparse autoencoder of a given size, how many tokens should you train on and so on.

cues.zh: 这对我们扩大这项工作规模帮助很大，也让我们更容易去训练真正大型的稀疏自编码器——不是训练大模型，而是开始到了训练真正大型模型变得昂贵的阶段。
cues.en: This was actually a very big help to us in scaling up this work, and made it a lot easier for us to go and train really large sparse autoencoders where it’s not training the big models, but it’s starting to get to a point where it’s actually expensive to go and train the really big ones.

cues.zh: 我的意思是，你得做所有这些把它拆分到大量 CPU 上的工作——
cues.en: I mean, you have to do all this stuff of splitting it across large CPUs-

cues.zh: 哦，是的。
cues.en: Oh, yeah.

cues.zh: 不，我是说这里也有巨大的工程挑战，对吧？
cues.en: No, I mean there’s a huge engineering challenge here too, right?

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 所以有一个科学问题：如何有效地扩展规模？
cues.en: So there’s a scientific question of how do you scale things effectively?

cues.zh: 然后还有大量的工程工作来扩大规模。
cues.en: And then there’s an enormous amount of engineering to go and scale this up.

cues.zh: 你得规划它，你得非常仔细地思考很多事情。
cues.en: You have to chart it, you have to think very carefully about a lot of things.

cues.zh: 我很幸运能和一群优秀的工程师共事，因为我绝对不是个优秀的工程师。
cues.en: I’m lucky to work with a bunch of great engineers because I am definitely not a great engineer.

cues.zh: 尤其是基础设施这块。
cues.en: And the infrastructure especially.

cues.zh: 没错，确实是这样。
cues.en: Yeah, for sure.

cues.zh: 所以简而言之，它奏效了。
cues.en: So it turns out TLDR, it worked.

cues.zh: 它奏效了。
cues.en: It worked.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我觉得这很重要，因为你本可以设想另一种情形：你朝着单语义性方向努力。
cues.en: And I think this is important because you could have imagined a world where you set after towards monospecificity.

cues.zh: Chris，这太棒了。
cues.en: Chris, this is great.

cues.zh: 它在单层模型上有效，但单层模型非常特殊。
cues.en: It works on a one-layer model, but one-layer models are really idiosyncratic.

cues.zh: 也许线性表示假说和叠加假说正是理解单层模型的正确方式，但并不是理解更大模型的正确方式。
cues.en: Maybe that’s just something, maybe the linear representation hypothesis and superposition hypothesis is the right way to understand a one-layer model, but it’s not the right way to understand larger models.

cues.zh: 所以我认为，首先，Cunningham等人的论文在一定程度上突破了这一点，并暗示情况并非如此。
cues.en: So I think, I mean, first of all, the Cunningham and all paper sort of cut through that a little bit and sort of suggested that this wasn’t the case.

cues.zh: 但《Scaling Monospecificity》我认为提供了重要证据，表明即使对非常大的模型也是如此，我们是在Claude 3 Sonnet上做的，当时它是我们的生产模型之一。
cues.en: But Scaling Monospecificity sort of I think was significant evidence that even for very large models, and we did it on Claude 3 Sonnet, which at that point was one of our production models.

cues.zh: 这些模型似乎基本上都能被解释清楚，至少通过线性特征可以做到。
cues.en: Even these models seemed to be substantially explained, at least by linear features.

cues.zh: 对它们做字典学习是有效的，而且随着你学到更多特征，你就能解释越来越多。
cues.en: And doing dictionary learning on them works, and as you learn more features, you go and you explain more and more.

cues.zh: 所以我觉得这是个相当有希望的迹象。
cues.en: So that’s, I think, quite a promising sign.

cues.zh: 你现在能发现真正迷人的抽象特征，而且这些特征还是多模态的。
cues.en: And you find now really fascinating abstract features, and the features are also multimodal.

cues.zh: 它们对同一概念的图像和文本都有响应，这很有意思。
cues.en: They respond to images and texts for the same concept, which is fun.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 你能解释一下吗？
cues.en: Can you explain that?

cues.zh: 我是说，后门，有很多例子你可以——
cues.en: I mean, backdoor, there’s just a lot of examples that you can-

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 那也许我们就从这开始吧。
cues.en: So maybe let’s start with that.

cues.zh: 先举一个例子，我们发现了一些围绕安全漏洞和代码后门植入的特征。
cues.en: One example to start, which is we found some features around security vulnerabilities and backdoorsing code.

cues.zh: 结果发现这其实是两个不同的特征。
cues.en: So turns out those are actually two different features.

cues.zh: 所以有一个安全漏洞特征，如果你强制激活它，Claude 就会开始往代码里写安全漏洞，比如缓冲区溢出。
cues.en: So there’s a security vulnerability feature, and if you force it active, Claude it will start to go and write security vulnerabilities like buffer overflows into code.

cues.zh: 它也会对各种情况触发，一些顶级数据集示例中会出现类似 --disable SSL 这样的东西，这些显然非常不安全。
cues.en: And also fires for all kinds of things, some of the top data set examples where things like dash dash, disable SSL or something like this, which are sort of obviously really insecure.

cues.zh: 所以到这一步，也许只是因为示例就是这样呈现的，暴露出来的是一些更表面、更明显的例子。
cues.en: So at this point, maybe it’s just because the examples are presented that way, it’s kind of surface a little bit more obvious examples.

cues.zh: 我猜这个想法是，后续它可能能够检测更细微的东西，比如欺骗或 bug 之类的。
cues.en: I guess the idea is that down the line it might be able to detect more nuance like deception or bugs or that kind of stuff.

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 也许我想区分两件事。
cues.en: Well, maybe I want to distinguish two things.

cues.zh: 一个是特征或概念的复杂度，对吧？
cues.en: So one is the complexity of the feature or the concept, right?

cues.zh: 另一个是我们所看示例的细微程度，对吧？
cues.en: And the other is the nuance of how subtle the examples we’re looking at, right?.

cues.zh: 当我们展示顶级数据集示例时，那些是导致该特征激活的最极端示例。
cues.en: So when we show the top data set examples, those are the most extreme examples that cause that feature to activate.

cues.zh: 所以这并不意味着它不会对更细微的情况触发。
cues.en: And so it doesn’t mean that it doesn’t fire for more subtle things.

cues.zh: 所以那个不安全代码特征，它最强烈触发的是一些非常明显的禁用安全类型的东西，但它也会对缓冲区溢出和代码中更微妙的安全漏洞触发。
cues.en: So that insecure code feature, the stuff that it fires most strongly for are these really obvious disable the security type things, but it also fires for buffer overflows and more subtle security vulnerabilities in code.

cues.zh: 这些特征都是多模态的。
cues.en: These features are all multimodal.

cues.zh: 你可以问它：“哪些图像会激活这个特征？”结果发现，安全漏洞特征会被人们点击 Chrome 越过这个网站的图像激活，可能是 SSL 证书有问题之类的。
cues.en: You could ask it like, “What images activate this feature?” And it turns out that the security vulnerability feature activates for images of people clicking on Chrome to go past this website, the SSL certificate might be wrong or something like this.

cues.zh: 另一件非常有趣的事是，代码中有后门特征，你激活它，Claude 就会写一个后门，把你的数据转储到端口之类的。
cues.en: Another thing that’s very entertaining is there’s backdoors in code feature, like you activate it, it goes and Claude writes a backdoor that will go and dump your data to port or something.

cues.zh: 但你可以问：“好吧，哪些图像会激活后门特征？”答案是那些内置隐藏摄像头的设备。
cues.en: But you can ask, “Okay, what images activate the backdoor feature?” It was devices with hidden cameras in them.

cues.zh: 所以显然存在一整类人，专门去卖看起来无害但内置隐藏摄像头的设备，而且他们的广告里还带着这个隐藏摄像头？
cues.en: So there’s a whole apparently genre of people going and selling devices that look innocuous that have hidden cameras, and they have ads that has this hidden camera in it?

cues.zh: 我猜那就是后门的物理版本。
cues.en: And I guess that is the physical version of a backdoor.

cues.zh: 所以这多少展示了这些概念有多抽象，我当时就觉得那挺……我有点难过，居然有一整个市场的人在卖那种设备，但我又有点高兴，因为它给出的该特征排名最高的图像示例就是这个。
cues.en: And so it sort of shows you how abstract these concepts are, and I just thought that was… I’m sort of sad that there’s a whole market of people selling devices like that, but I was kind of delighted that that was the thing that it came up with as the top image examples for the feature.

cues.zh: 是啊，挺好的。
cues.en: Yeah, it’s nice.

cues.zh: 它是多模态的。
cues.en: It’s multimodal.

cues.zh: 它几乎是多上下文的。
cues.en: It’s multi almost context.

cues.zh: 它是对单一概念的宽泛而强烈的定义。
cues.en: It’s broad, strong definition of a singular concept.

cues.zh: 这很好。
cues.en: It’s nice.

cues.zh: 是啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 对我来说，一个特别有意思的特性，尤其是对 AI 安全而言，就是欺骗和撒谎。
cues.en: To me, one of the really interesting features, especially for AI safety, is deception and lying.

cues.zh: 以及这类方法有可能检测出模型在撒谎，尤其是模型变得越来越聪明。
cues.en: And the possibility that these kinds of methods could detect lying in a model, especially get smarter and smarter and smarter.

cues.zh: 想必这对超级智能模型是个巨大威胁——它可能就自身意图之类的东西欺骗操作它的人。
cues.en: Presumably that’s a big threat over super intelligent model that it can deceive the people operating it as to its intentions or any of that kind of stuff.

cues.zh: 那么，你们从检测模型内部撒谎中学到了什么？
cues.en: So what have you learned from detecting lying inside models?

cues.zh: 是啊，我觉得这方面某种程度上还处于早期阶段，我们发现了不少与欺骗和撒谎相关的特征。
cues.en: Yeah, so I think we’re in some ways in early days for that, we find quite a few features related to deception and lying.

cues.zh: 有一个特征会在人们撒谎和欺骗时被激活，你强行把它激活，Claude 就开始对你撒谎。
cues.en: There’s one feature where it fires for people lying and being deceptive, and you force it active and Claude starts lying to you.

cues.zh: 所以我们有一个欺骗特征。
cues.en: So we have a deception feature.

cues.zh: 我是说，还有各种其他特征，比如隐瞒信息、不回答问题，还有追求权力、搞政变之类的特征。
cues.en: I mean, there’s all kinds of other features about withholding information and not answering questions, features about power seeking and coups and stuff like that.

cues.zh: 所以有很多特征跟那些诡异的东西相关，如果你强行激活它们，Claude 的行为就会变得……那不是你想要的行为。
cues.en: So there’s a lot of features that are kind of related to spooky things, and if you force them active Claude will behave in ways that are… they’re not the kinds of behaviors you want.

cues.zh: 在 Mechinterp 领域，你觉得接下来有哪些令人兴奋的方向？
cues.en: What are possible next exciting directions to you in the space of Mechinterp?

cues.zh: 嗯，有很多。
cues.en: Well, there’s a lot of things.

cues.zh: 首先，我真的很希望能达到这样一个阶段：我们有了捷径，不仅能真正理解特征，还能用它来理解模型的计算过程。
cues.en: So for one thing, I would really like to get to a point where we have shortcuts where we can really understand not just the features, but then use that to understand the computation of models.

cues.zh: 那种释然对我来说就是这项工作的终极目标。
cues.en: That relief for me is the ultimate goal of this.

cues.zh: 已经有一些工作了，我们发布了一些东西。
cues.en: And there’s been some work, we put out a few things.

cues.zh: Sam Marks 有一篇论文做了类似的事情，而且在这个边缘领域已经有一些工作了。
cues.en: There’s a paper from Sam Marks that does some stuff like this, and there’s been, I’d say some work around the edges here.

cues.zh: 但我觉得还有很多事要做，我认为这会是一个非常令人兴奋的方向，和我们称之为“干扰权重”的挑战有关。
cues.en: But I think there’s a lot more to do, and I think that will be a very exciting thing that’s related to a challenge we call interference weights.

cues.zh: 由于叠加现象，如果你只是天真地看哪些特征连在一起，可能有些权重在上层模型中并不存在，而只是叠加产生的伪影。
cues.en: Where due to superstition, if you just sort of naively look at what features are connected together, there may be some weights that don’t exist in the upstairs model, but are just sort of artifacts of superstition.

cues.zh: 所以这是一个技术挑战。与此相关，我觉得另一个令人兴奋的方向是，你可以把稀疏自编码器想象成某种望远镜。
cues.en: So that’s a technical challenge Related to that, I think another exciting direction is just you might think of sparse autoencoders as being kind of like a telescope.

cues.zh: 它们让我们能向外看，看到外面所有这些特征，而随着我们构建越来越好的稀疏自编码器、越来越擅长字典学习，我们就能看到越来越多的星星。
cues.en: They allow us to look out and see all these features that are out there, and as we build better and better sparse autoencoders, we better and better at dictionary learning, we see more and more stars.

cues.zh: 我们不断放大，观察越来越小的星体。
cues.en: And we zoom in on smaller and smaller stars.

cues.zh: 有很多证据表明，我们目前看到的还只是极小一部分星体。
cues.en: There’s a lot of evidence that we’re only still seeing a very small fraction of the stars.

cues.zh: 在我们的神经网络宇宙中，有大量物质是我们现在还观测不到的。
cues.en: There’s a lot of matter in our neural network universe that we can’t observe yet.

cues.zh: 也许我们永远都无法拥有足够精细的仪器去观测它，而且有些东西可能根本就不可能、在计算上也无法观测。
cues.en: And it may be that we’ll never be able to have fine enough instruments to observe it, and maybe some of it just isn’t possible, isn’t computationally tractable to observe.

cues.zh: 所以这有点像暗物质，不过也许不是现代天文学意义上的暗物质，而是早期天文学那种——我们不知道这种无法解释的物质是什么。
cues.en: So it’s sort of a kind of dark matter in not in maybe the sense of modern astronomy of early astronomy when we didn’t know what this unexplained matter is.

cues.zh: 所以我经常思考那种暗物质，思考我们是否终将观测到它，以及如果我们观测不到、如果神经网络中有相当一部分是我们无法触及的，这对安全性意味着什么。
cues.en: And so I think a lot about that dark matter and whether we’ll ever observe it and what that means for safety if we can’t observe it, if some significant fraction of neural networks are not accessible to us.

cues.zh: 我经常思考的另一个问题是，说到底，机制性插值是一种非常微观的插值方法。
cues.en: Another question that I think a lot about is at the end of the day, mechanistic interpolation is this very microscopic approach to interpolation.

cues.zh: 它试图以非常细粒度的方式理解事物，但我们关心的很多问题都是非常宏观的。
cues.en: It’s trying to understand things in a very fine-grained way, but a lot of the questions we care about are very macroscopic.

cues.zh: 我们关心的是关于神经网络行为的这些问题，我想这是我最关心的事。
cues.en: We care about these questions about neural network behavior, and I think that’s the thing that I care most about.

cues.zh: 但你可能关心的还有很多其他更大尺度的问题。
cues.en: But there’s lots of other sort of larger-scale questions you might care about.

cues.zh: 采用非常微观的方法的好处是，可能更容易问：这是真的吗？
cues.en: And the nice thing about having a very microscopic approach is it’s maybe easier to ask, is this true?

cues.zh: 但缺点是，它离我们关心的事情远得多。
cues.en: But the downside is its much further from the things we care about.

cues.zh: 所以我们现在有这架梯子要爬。
cues.en: And so we now have this ladder to climb.

cues.zh: 我认为有一个问题是，我们能否找到——是否存在更大尺度的抽象，可以用来理解神经网络，让我们能从这个非常微观的方法往上走？
cues.en: And I think there’s a question of will we be able to find, are there larger-scale abstractions that we can use to understand neural networks that can we get up from this very microscopic approach?

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 你写过这方面的内容，把它比作器官问题。
cues.en: You’ve written about this as kind of organs question.

cues.zh: 是的，没错。
cues.en: Yeah, exactly.

cues.zh: 如果我们把可解释性看作神经网络的一种解剖学，大多数研究线索都涉及研究微小的血管，关注小尺度和单个神经元以及它们如何连接。
cues.en: If we think of interpretability as a kind of anatomy of neural networks, most of the circus threads involve studying tiny little veins looking at the small scale and individual neurons and how they connect.

cues.zh: 然而，有许多自然的问题是小尺度方法无法解决的。
cues.en: However, there are many natural questions that the small-scale approach doesn’t address.

cues.zh: 相比之下，最突出的抽象和生物解剖学涉及更大规模的结构，比如单个器官，如心脏，或整个器官系统，如呼吸系统。
cues.en: In contrast, the most prominent abstractions and biological anatomy involve larger-scale structures like individual organs, like the heart or entire organ systems like the respiratory system.

cues.zh: 所以我们想知道，人工神经网络中是否存在呼吸系统、心脏或大脑区域？
cues.en: And so we wonder, is there a respiratory system or heart or brain region of an artificial neural network?

cues.zh: 是的，没错。
cues.en: Yeah, exactly.

cues.zh: 我的意思是，如果你想想科学，对吧？
cues.en: And I mean, if you think about science, right?

cues.zh: 很多科学领域都会在多个抽象层次上研究事物。
cues.en: A lot of scientific fields investigate things at many level of abstraction.

cues.zh: 在生物学中，有研究蛋白质和分子等的分子生物学，还有细胞生物学，然后是研究组织的组织学，再然后是解剖学，再然后是动物学，再然后是生态学。
cues.en: In biology, you have molecular biology studying proteins and molecules and so on, and they have cellular biology, and then you have histology studying tissues, and then you have anatomy, and then you have zoology, and then you have ecology.

cues.zh: 所以有很多很多抽象层次，或者物理学，也许有单个粒子的物理学，然后统计物理给出热力学之类的东西。
cues.en: And so you have many, many levels of abstraction or physics, maybe you have a physics of individual particles, and then statistical physics gives you thermodynamics and things like this.

cues.zh: 所以你经常会有不同的抽象层次。
cues.en: And so you often have different levels of abstraction.

cues.zh: 我认为现在我们有机制可解释性，如果它成功的话，有点像神经网络的微生物学，但我们想要更像解剖学的东西。
cues.en: And I think that right now we have mechanistic interpretability, if it succeeds, is sort of like a microbiology of neural networks, but we want something more like anatomy.

cues.zh: 你可能会问：“为什么不能直接去那里？”我认为答案很大程度上是迷信。
cues.en: And a question you might ask is, “Why can’t you just go there directly?” And I think the answer is superstition, at least in significant part.

cues.zh: 实际上，如果不先以正确的方式拆解微观结构，再研究它们如何连接，就很难看清这种宏观结构。
cues.en: It’s that it’s actually very hard to see this macroscopic structure without first sort of breaking down the microscopic structure in the right way and then studying how it connects together.

cues.zh: 但我希望会有比特征和电路大得多的东西，我们将能够讲述一个涉及更大事物的故事。
cues.en: But I’m hopeful that there is going to be something much larger than features and circuits and that we’re going to be able to have a story that involves much bigger things.

cues.zh: 然后你就可以详细研究你关心的部分。
cues.en: And then you can sort of study in detail the parts you care about.

cues.zh: 我想，在你的生物学中，就像神经网络的心理学家或精神病学家。
cues.en: I suppose, in your biology, like a psychologist or a psychiatrist of a neural network.

cues.zh: 我认为美妙之处在于，如果我们能去做，而不是为这两件事设立不同的领域，如果你能在它们之间架起一座桥梁，这样你就能让你所有更高层次的抽象都牢牢扎根于这个非常坚实、更严谨、理想情况下是基础的东西上。
cues.en: And I think that the beautiful thing would be if we could go and rather than having disparate fields for those two things, if you could build a bridge between them, such that you could go and have all of your higher level distractions be grounded very firmly in this very solid, more rigorous, ideally foundation.

cues.zh: 你认为人脑、生物神经网络和人工神经网络之间的区别是什么？
cues.en: What do you think is the difference between the human brain, the biological neural network and the artificial neural network?

cues.zh: 嗯，神经科学家的工作比我们难得多。
cues.en: Well, the neuroscientists have a much harder job than us.

cues.zh: 有时我庆幸自己的活儿比神经科学家轻松太多了。
cues.en: Sometimes I just count my blessings by how much easier my job is than the neuroscientists.

cues.zh: 我们可以记录所有神经元的活动。
cues.en: So we can record from all the neurons.

cues.zh: 我们能在任意规模的数据上做到这一点。
cues.en: We can do that on arbitrary amounts of data.

cues.zh: 顺便说一句，做这些的时候神经元本身不会改变。
cues.en: The neurons don’t change while you’re doing that, by the way.

cues.zh: 你可以去消融神经元，可以编辑连接等等，然后还能撤销这些改动。
cues.en: You can go and ablate neurons, you can edit the connections and so on, and then you can undo those changes.

cues.zh: 这相当棒。
cues.en: That’s pretty great.

cues.zh: 你可以干预任意神经元，强制它激活，看看会发生什么。
cues.en: You can intervene on any neuron and force it active and see what happens.

cues.zh: 你知道哪些神经元与所有东西相连。
cues.en: You know which neurons are connected to everything.

cues.zh: 神经科学家想获得连接组，而我们已经有连接组了，而且规模比 C 大得多。
cues.en: Neuroscientists want to get the connectome, we have the connectome and we have it for much bigger than C.

cues.zh: elegans。
cues.en: elegans.

cues.zh: 然后我们不仅有连接组，还知道哪些神经元之间是兴奋或抑制关系，对吧？
cues.en: And then not only do we have the connectome, we know which neurons excite or inhibit each other, right?

cues.zh: 不只是知道二值掩码，我们还知道权重。
cues.en: It’s not just that we know the binary mask, we know the weights.

cues.zh: 我们可以求梯度，从计算上知道每个神经元在做什么。
cues.en: We can take gradients, we know computationally what each neuron does.

cues.zh: 我不知道。
cues.en: I don’t know.

cues.zh: 这样的优势还能列很多。
cues.en: The list goes on and on.

cues.zh: 相比神经科学家，我们就是有太多优势了。
cues.en: We just have so many advantages over neuroscientists.

cues.zh: 可即便有这么多优势，这事还是很难。
cues.en: And then despite having all those advantages, it’s really hard.

cues.zh: 所以我有时会想：“天哪，如果对我们都这么难，那在神经科学的约束下似乎就是不可能，或者近乎不可能。”我不知道。
cues.en: And so one thing I do sometimes think is like, “Gosh, if it’s this hard for us, it seems impossible under the constraints of neuroscience or near impossible.” I don’t know.

cues.zh: 也许我的一部分想法是，我团队里有几位神经科学家，我可能有点想说：“啊，神经科学家们。
cues.en: Maybe part of me is I’ve got a few neuroscientists on my team, maybe I’m sort of like, “Ah, the neuroscientists.

cues.zh: 也许他们中有些人会想要一个更简单、但仍然很难的问题，然后可以来研究神经网络。
cues.en: Maybe some of them would like to have an easier problem that’s still very hard, and they could come and work on neural networks.

cues.zh: 然后，等我们在理解神经网络这个相对简单的小池塘里把问题搞清楚——这本身仍然非常困难——之后，我们就能回到生物神经科学了。”
cues.en: And then after we figure out things in sort of the easy little pond of trying to understand neural networks, which is still very hard, then we could go back to biological neuroscience.”

cues.zh: 我很喜欢你写的关于 MechInterp 研究目标的两点：安全性和美感。
cues.en: I love what you’ve written about the goal of MechInterp research as two goals, safety and beauty.

cues.zh: 那你能谈谈美感这一面吗？
cues.en: So can you talk about the beauty side of things?

cues.zh: 好啊。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 有个有趣的现象，我觉得有些人对神经网络有点失望，他们会说：“唉，神经网络，不就是这些简单的规则嘛。
cues.en: So there’s this funny thing where I think some people are kind of disappointed by neural networks, I think, where they’re like, “Ah, neural networks, it’s just these simple rules.

cues.zh: 然后你只要做一堆工程把它扩展起来，效果就很好。
cues.en: Then you just do a bunch of engineering to scale it up and it works really well.

cues.zh: 那复杂的想法在哪呢？
cues.en: And where’s the complex ideas?

cues.zh: 这算不上什么漂亮、优美的科学成果。”我有时觉得，人们这么说的时候，我脑海里浮现出他们像是在说：“进化论太无聊了。
cues.en: This isn’t a very nice, beautiful scientific result.” And I sometimes think when people say that, I picture them being like, “Evolution is so boring.

cues.zh: 不过就是一堆简单的规则。
cues.en: It’s just a bunch of simple rules.

cues.zh: 让进化运行很长时间，就得到了生物学。
cues.en: And you run evolution for a long time and you get biology.

cues.zh: 生物学最后演化成这样，也太糟糕了。
cues.en: What a sucky way for biology to have turned out.

cues.zh: “复杂的规则在哪？”但美妙之处在于，简单能生成复杂。
cues.en: Where’s the complex rules?” But the beauty is that the simplicity generates complexity.

cues.zh: 生物学有这些简单的规则，却孕育出我们周围所见的一切生命和生态系统。
cues.en: Biology has these simple rules and it gives rise to all the life and ecosystems that we see around us.

cues.zh: 大自然所有的美，都来自进化，来自进化中某种非常简单的机制。
cues.en: All the beauty of nature, that all just comes from evolution and from something very simple in evolution.

cues.zh: 同样地，我认为神经网络在自身内部构建、创造出巨大的复杂性和美感，以及内部结构，而人们通常不去看、也不试图理解，因为很难理解。
cues.en: And similarly, I think that neural networks build, create enormous complexity and beauty inside and structure inside themselves that people generally don’t look at and don’t try to understand because it’s hard to understand.

cues.zh: 但我认为，神经网络内部有极其丰富的结构等待被发现，有大量非常深邃的美，只要我们愿意花时间去观察和理解。
cues.en: But I think that there is an incredibly rich structure to be discovered inside neural networks, a lot of very deep beauty if we’re just willing to take the time to go and see it and understand it.

cues.zh: 是的，我热爱机制可解释性。
cues.en: Yeah, I love Mechinterp.

cues.zh: 那种感觉就像我们正在理解，或者隐约窥见内部运作的魔法，真的很美妙。
cues.en: The feeling like we are understanding or getting glimpses of understanding the magic that’s going on inside is really wonderful.

cues.zh: 对我来说，这就像是一个亟待提出的问题，我的意思是，很多人都在思考这个问题，但我常常感到惊讶的是，为什么没有更多人问：我们怎么还不知道如何创建能做这些事的计算机系统？
cues.en: It feels to me like one of the questions that’s just calling out to be asked, and I’m sort of, I mean a lot of people are thinking about this, but I’m often surprised that not more are is how is it that we don’t know how to create computer systems that can do these things?

cues.zh: 然而我们已经有这些惊人的系统，我们不知道如何直接编写能完成这些事情的计算机程序，但这些神经网络却能完成所有这些惊人的事情。
cues.en: And yet we have these amazing systems that we don’t know how to directly create computer programs that can do these things, but these neural networks can do all these amazing things.

cues.zh: 感觉这显然就是一个亟待回答的问题。
cues.en: And it just feels like that is obviously the question that is calling out to be answered.

cues.zh: 如果你有任何程度的好奇心，就会想：“人类怎么现在拥有了这些能做我们不知道怎么做的事情的造物？”
cues.en: If you have any degree of curiosity, it’s like, “How is it that humanity now has these artifacts that can do these things that we don’t know how to do?”

cues.zh: 是的。
cues.en: Yeah.

cues.zh: 我喜欢马戏团向着目标函数之光伸展的画面。
cues.en: I love the image of the circus reaching towards the light of the objective function.

cues.zh: 是的，这是我们培育出来的有机体，而我们根本不知道培育出了什么。
cues.en: Yeah, it’s this organic thing that we’ve grown and we have no idea what we’ve grown.

cues.zh: 感谢你致力于安全研究，也感谢你欣赏你所发现之物的美。
cues.en: Well, thank you for working on safety, and thank you for appreciating the beauty of the things you discover.

cues.zh: Chris，谢谢你今天的对谈，非常精彩。
cues.en: And thank you for talking today, Chris, this was wonderful.

cues.zh: 也谢谢你抽出时间来聊天。
cues.en: Thank you for taking the time to chat as well.

cues.zh: 感谢收听与 Chris Ola 的对话，以及此前与 Dario Amodei 和 Amanda Askell 的对话。
cues.en: Thanks for listening to this conversation with Chris Ola and before that, with Dario Amodei and Amanda Askell.

cues.zh: 想支持本播客，请查看简介中的赞助商。
cues.en: To support this podcast, please check out our sponsors in the description.

cues.zh: 最后，让我用 Alan Watts 的一段话作结。
cues.en: And now let me leave you with some words from Alan Watts.

cues.zh: “要理解变化，唯一的办法就是投身其中，与它同行，加入这场舞蹈。”感谢收听，期待下次再见。
cues.en: “The only way to make sense out of change is to plunge into it, move with it, and join the dance.” Thank you for listening and hope to see you next time.
